guides.title: Conduction, Convection and Radiant Heat
guides.summary: The three mechanisms that carry energy into food, treated as a working diagnostic: what each one physically is, the numbers that govern it, how to tell which is doing the work in any given setup, and how to change the dominant mode when the result is wrong.

sections.heading: Three Mechanisms, and Why Naming Them Changes What You Do
sections.body: Energy can reach a piece of food in exactly three ways, and no more. It can be handed along through touching matter without the matter itself travelling, which is conduction. It can be carried by a moving fluid — air, water, oil, steam — which is convection. Or it can arrive as electromagnetic radiation, crossing empty space at the speed of light and depositing energy when it is absorbed, which is thermal radiation. Every cooking process ever devised is some combination of those three, weighted differently. This is not a taxonomy for its own sake. It is the most useful diagnostic in the kitchen, because each mode obeys different rules, responds to different interventions, and fails in a different characteristic way. If a steak is grey and weeping rather than brown and crusted, that is a convection and radiation problem at the surface, and turning up the oven will not fix it. If a chicken thigh is charred outside and raw at the bone, that is a conduction problem inside the meat, and no adjustment to the heat source will fix it either — the only levers are lower external temperature and more time, or a smaller piece. If one tray of biscuits browns and the next does not, the likely cause is radiation view factor and tray colour, not the thermostat. Diagnosing the mode also tells you which quantity to change. Conduction depends on the material and on thickness. Convection depends on fluid motion and on which fluid. Radiation depends on temperature raised to the fourth power, on surface colour and finish, and on what can see what. These are largely independent knobs, and pushing the wrong one is the commonest reason a cook repeats a failure while feeling they have tried everything. One clarification prevents most confusion downstream. Heat is energy in transit because of a temperature difference; temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance. A domestic oven at 200 degrees Celsius and a pan of oil at 200 degrees are at the same temperature and deliver energy at wildly different rates, because air is thin and moves slowly past the food while oil is dense and clings. Temperature tells you which direction energy flows and sets the ceiling; it does not tell you how fast. Everything interesting about cooking lies in the rate, and the rate is what the three mechanisms describe. A fourth process, phase change, is often listed alongside these, but it is not a separate transport mechanism. Evaporation and condensation move energy in bulk as latent heat, and they interact powerfully with all three modes — usually by pinning a wet surface near 100 degrees Celsius no matter how hard you heat it.

sections.heading: Conduction: What Is Actually Being Passed Along
sections.body: Conduction is energy transfer through matter by direct molecular interaction, with no net movement of the material itself. Two distinct physical mechanisms produce it, and knowing which is operating explains the enormous spread of conductivity between materials. In any solid, atoms are bound to their neighbours and vibrate about fixed positions. Heating one end makes those atoms vibrate more vigorously, and because they are coupled to their neighbours the agitation propagates as elastic waves through the lattice. Physicists quantise these vibrations and call the quanta phonons. Phonon conduction operates in every solid — metal, ceramic, glass, ice, meat — and it is comparatively slow, because energy is handed on collision by collision and phonons scatter off defects, grain boundaries and each other. Metals add a second and far more effective channel. In a metal, the outer electrons are not bound to individual atoms but form a delocalised sea that moves freely through the lattice. These electrons are light, fast, and travel long distances between collisions, carrying kinetic energy with them. This is why the best conductors of heat are also the best conductors of electricity: both properties depend on the same mobile electrons, a relationship formalised in the Wiedemann–Franz law, which states that the ratio of thermal to electrical conductivity is roughly proportional to absolute temperature and nearly the same constant for all metals. The numbers, in watts per metre per kelvin, span four orders of magnitude and are worth committing roughly to memory. Copper is about 400, aluminium about 235, cast iron around 50, carbon steel about 45, stainless steel only 15 to 16, glass and ceramic 1 to 1.4, water 0.6, fat and oil around 0.17, dry air 0.026. Foods sit low: lean meat is about 0.45 to 0.5, largely because it is mostly water, potato around 0.55, bread about 0.05 because it is mostly trapped air, and fat well under half the value of lean tissue. Two consequences follow immediately. First, stainless steel is a poor conductor — about twenty-five times worse than copper — which is why quality stainless pans are built as a sandwich with an aluminium or copper core; the steel provides the durable, non-reactive, magnetic surfaces and the core does the actual heat spreading. Second, food is a thermal insulator. Meat conducts roughly a thousand times worse than copper. Heat entering a roast crawls inward, and this single fact sets the pace of nearly all cooking of solid pieces: the outside is always hotter than the inside, the gradient is steep, and no amount of external power changes the internal rate — it only makes the gradient steeper and burns the outside sooner. Fat insulates better still, which is part of why a fatty joint cooks more slowly than a lean one of the same weight, and why bone, being denser and better conducting than the meat around it, can leave a locally faster-cooking channel.

sections.heading: Fourier's Law and the Numbers That Govern a Pan
sections.body: The quantitative statement of conduction was published by Joseph Fourier in 1822 and is simple enough to use directly. The rate of heat flow through a slab equals the thermal conductivity of the material, times the cross-sectional area, times the temperature difference across it, divided by the thickness. Written compactly, Q equals k A delta T over L, with Q in watts. Every term is a lever. Doubling the temperature difference doubles the flow. Doubling the area doubles it. Doubling the thickness halves it. Changing the material changes k, and as the range from copper at 400 to air at 0.026 shows, that is the most powerful lever available. A worked example makes it concrete. Take a cast-iron pan base 5 millimetres thick with a heated area of 0.03 square metres, k about 50, and a temperature difference of 10 degrees across the metal. The flow is 50 times 0.03 times 10 divided by 0.005, which equals 3,000 watts. That is comfortably more than a domestic burner delivers, which tells you something useful: the metal is not the bottleneck. The pan base can pass far more power than the burner supplies, so the temperature drop across the metal is small. The bottleneck lies elsewhere — in the contact with the food, in the burner itself, or in the food's own conduction. Now run the same calculation for a 25-millimetre-thick steak, k about 0.45, area 0.01 square metres, with the surface at 180 degrees and the centre at 20. The flow is 0.45 times 0.01 times 160 divided by 0.025, or about 29 watts. The contrast with 3,000 watts is the entire story of why cooking a thick piece of meat takes time. The food is the resistor. The idea of thermal resistance makes this systematic. Rearranged, Fourier's law says flow equals temperature difference divided by resistance, where resistance equals L over k A — exactly parallel to Ohm's law for electricity. Resistances in series add, so a stack of layers is easy to analyse: the layer with the largest resistance dominates, and improving any other layer is wasted effort. This is why a copper pan with a thick layer of burnt-on residue performs badly, why an oven glove of a few millimetres of trapped air works at all, and why a thin film of steam or fat between food and pan can matter more than the pan's material. One caution: k varies with temperature and, in foods, changes dramatically on freezing, because ice conducts about four times better than liquid water. A frozen item conducts heat inward much faster than the same item thawed, which is why frozen food thaws from the outside slowly but, once thawing, slows further.

sections.heading: Contact Resistance: The Gap You Cannot See
sections.body: Fourier's law assumes layers are in perfect thermal contact. They almost never are, and the gap is responsible for a large share of frustrating kitchen results. Press two solid surfaces together and, however smooth they look, they touch only at scattered high points. Real contact area is typically a small percentage of apparent area; the rest is a thin layer of whatever fluid occupies the space, usually air. Since air conducts at 0.026 watts per metre per kelvin, roughly two thousand times worse than aluminium, that microscopic gap can be the dominant resistance in the entire path. Engineers call this thermal contact resistance, and they defeat it with thermal paste. Cooks defeat it with fat. This explains a set of otherwise puzzling observations. A steak laid on a hot pan touches it only at a few points, because neither surface is flat at the microscopic scale and meat is stiff when cold. A film of oil fills the voids, and although oil's conductivity of about 0.17 is unimpressive in absolute terms, it is roughly seven times better than air and, crucially, it wets both surfaces so the gap disappears. This is the main reason a lightly oiled pan sears far better than a dry one, quite apart from any effect on sticking. The same logic explains warped pans. A base that has bowed even half a millimetre may touch an induction hob or electric plate only around its rim, so the centre receives energy almost entirely by radiation and by conduction through air, and the pan develops a persistent cold spot. On gas this matters less, because the flame heats the underside directly by convection and radiation regardless of contact. It explains why a wire rack changes roasting. Food sitting directly on a solid tray conducts into the metal across a large contact patch, and the underside behaves quite differently from the top. On a rack, contact is reduced to a few thin lines, and the underside is exposed to the same convective and radiant environment as everything else, giving even browning all round. It explains why pressing food with a weight or a press works — increasing the force flattens the high points, increases genuine contact area and reduces the resistance — and why a thick, flat, heavy pan sears better than a thin one, since a thin base flexes away from the food as it heats unevenly. And it explains why the first thirty seconds of contact are often the most important. Cold food draws heat from the pan surface faster than the burner can resupply it, so surface temperature drops sharply — a phenomenon governed by thermal effusivity, the product of conductivity, density and specific heat capacity, which measures how readily a material exchanges heat at an interface. Cast iron has high effusivity and holds its surface temperature; thin aluminium does not. That initial drop, not the set temperature, is what determines whether a crust starts to form.

sections.heading: Transient Conduction: Why Thickness Is Squared
sections.body: Fourier's law describes steady flow, but cooking is almost never steady. What matters is how a temperature front moves into a cold object, and that behaviour follows a different and rather unforgiving rule. The governing property is thermal diffusivity, written alpha, defined as conductivity divided by the product of density and specific heat capacity. Conductivity says how readily energy flows; density and heat capacity say how much energy must be deposited to raise the temperature. Their ratio says how fast a temperature change propagates. Its units are square metres per second, and the appearance of square metres is the crucial clue. Values are instructive. Copper is about 1.1 times 10 to the minus 4 square metres per second. Water is about 1.4 times 10 to the minus 7, roughly eight hundred times slower. Most raw foods cluster near 1.3 to 1.6 times 10 to the minus 7, because they are mostly water. Fat is somewhat lower, and air, despite conducting badly, has a high diffusivity of about 2 times 10 to the minus 5 because it stores so little energy per unit volume. Because alpha has units of length squared over time, the characteristic time for heat to penetrate a distance L scales as L squared divided by alpha. This is the square law, and it is the single most useful piece of arithmetic in cooking timing. Double the thickness of a piece of meat and the time to heat its centre goes up roughly fourfold, not twofold. Halve the thickness and you quarter the time. Check it against experience. A 25-millimetre steak needs heat to travel about 12.5 millimetres to the centre from both sides. With alpha of 1.4 times 10 to the minus 7, L squared over alpha is 0.0125 squared divided by 1.4 times 10 to the minus 7, which is about 1,100 seconds, or roughly 19 minutes. Real steaks cook faster because that formula gives a full-equilibration timescale and the centre only needs to reach a target well below the surface temperature, but the scaling is right, and it correctly predicts that a 50-millimetre steak needs about four times as long. Two dimensionless numbers formalise the picture. The Biot number compares external heat delivery to internal conduction: it is h L over k, where h is the surface heat transfer coefficient. When Biot is much less than about 0.1, the inside conducts far faster than the outside supplies, so the object heats almost uniformly — true for a thin piece of metal, rarely true for food. When Biot is large, as it is for a roast in a hot oven, the surface races ahead and steep internal gradients form. The Fourier number, alpha t over L squared, is dimensionless time; equal Fourier numbers mean equal progress toward equilibrium, which is why geometrically similar pieces of the same food scale predictably.

sections.heading: Convection: The Boundary Layer Is the Whole Story
sections.body: Convection is heat transfer by a moving fluid, and it is best understood as conduction through a thin stagnant film, with the fluid's motion controlling how thin that film is. A fluid flowing past a solid surface does not slip at the wall. Right at the surface, velocity is zero — the no-slip condition — and it rises to the free-stream value over a short distance called the boundary layer. Within that layer, and especially in the sublayer closest to the wall, the fluid barely moves, so energy must cross it by conduction through a poor conductor. This film is the dominant resistance in nearly every convective situation. Stirring, blowing, pumping and whisking all work by the same means: they thin the boundary layer. The bookkeeping is done with Newton's law of cooling, which states that the heat flow equals the heat transfer coefficient h, times the area, times the difference between the surface temperature and the bulk fluid temperature. The coefficient h bundles all the messy fluid dynamics into one number, in watts per square metre per kelvin, and its value spans an enormous range. Typical figures are worth knowing because they explain why identical temperatures cook so differently. Still air gives h of roughly 5 to 15. Air moved by a fan gives 20 to 60. Boiling water gives about 1,000 to 3,000. Hot oil in a deep fryer gives 250 to 1,000, higher once vigorous bubbling from the food's own moisture stirs it. Condensing steam is extraordinary, at 5,000 to 15,000 or more. Water at 100 degrees therefore delivers energy some hundred times faster than air at 100 degrees, which is why you can hold your hand in a 120-degree oven for a moment but not in boiling water, and why steam scalds so severely. The dimensionless group that describes convection is the Nusselt number, the ratio of actual convective transfer to what pure conduction through the same fluid layer would give: Nu equals h L over k of the fluid. A Nusselt number of 1 means the fluid might as well be stationary; large Nusselt numbers mean motion is doing real work. Engineering correlations predict Nu from other dimensionless groups, and h is then recovered from it. The practical rules that follow are direct. Anything that keeps fluid still — crowding a pan, piling food in a fryer basket, packing a steamer — thickens boundary layers and slows cooking far more than the temperature drop alone would suggest. Anything that renews the fluid at the surface speeds it: stirring a sauce, spacing items on a tray, turning food, or shaking a basket. And a food surface's own escaping steam forms an insulating layer, which is one reason a wet surface browns so reluctantly.

sections.heading: Natural Against Forced Convection, and What a Fan Really Does
sections.body: Convection comes in two kinds, distinguished by what drives the motion, and they behave differently enough that treating them as one thing causes real errors. Natural or free convection is driven by buoyancy. Fluid touching a hot surface warms, expands, becomes less dense and rises, drawing cooler fluid in behind it. The circulation is self-generated and gentle, with air speeds in a domestic oven typically of the order of 0.1 to 0.5 metres per second. Its strength is captured by the Rayleigh number, the product of the Grashof number — which compares buoyancy to viscous damping — and the Prandtl number, which compares how readily a fluid diffuses momentum against heat. Below a Rayleigh number of about 10 to the 9th the flow is laminar and orderly; above it, turbulent and more effective. Forced convection is driven by an external device: a fan, a pump, a whisk, a draught. Speeds rise to several metres per second, and h rises with them, typically as velocity to the power of about 0.5 to 0.8 rather than linearly, so doubling fan speed increases transfer by perhaps 50 to 70 percent rather than doubling it. This is what a fan oven does, and it is worth stating precisely because it is widely misdescribed. A fan does not make the oven hotter; a fan oven set to 180 degrees contains air at 180 degrees just as a conventional one does. What it does is raise h from roughly 10 to roughly 30 or more, so the same air temperature delivers energy two to three times faster. It also destroys the strong vertical temperature stratification of a still oven, in which the top can sit 20 to 30 degrees above the bottom, giving even results across several shelves. The standard advice to reduce the set temperature by about 20 degrees Celsius when using a fan follows directly. You are compensating for a higher h by lowering delta T so the product, and therefore the surface heating rate, comes out similar. The advice is approximate because the two are not equivalent in their effects: the fan also accelerates evaporation from the surface, which dries and browns exteriors more aggressively. That is desirable for roast potatoes and pastry and undesirable for a delicate custard or a rich fruit cake, which is why some recipes specify conventional heat deliberately. Forced convection also explains wind chill and its kitchen analogues. A cold draught across a cooling tray dramatically speeds cooling; a chest freezer with a fan freezes faster than one without at the same temperature; blowing on hot soup works by thinning the boundary layer at the surface as well as by carrying away vapour. One asymmetry is worth remembering: natural convection depends on gravity and on the temperature difference itself, so it weakens as the food approaches the oven temperature, while forced convection does not. Long, low-temperature cooking in a still oven therefore slows disproportionately at the end.

sections.heading: Radiation: The Fourth-Power Law and the Invisible Half of an Oven
sections.body: Radiation is the odd one out. It needs no medium, travels at the speed of light, and is governed by a law so steep that it changes character entirely across the range of temperatures a kitchen spans. Every object above absolute zero emits electromagnetic radiation because its charged particles are in constant thermal motion, and accelerating charges radiate. The total power emitted per unit area is given by the Stefan–Boltzmann law: it equals emissivity times the Stefan–Boltzmann constant, 5.67 times 10 to the minus 8 watts per square metre per kelvin to the fourth, times absolute temperature to the fourth power. Absolute temperature means kelvin, and the fourth power is what makes radiation dramatic. Work an example. A grill element glowing at 800 degrees Celsius is 1,073 kelvin. Food at 20 degrees is 293 kelvin. Net exchange goes as the difference of the fourth powers, and 1,073 to the fourth is about 1.33 times 10 to the 12, against 7.4 times 10 to the 9 for the food — a ratio near 180. The element radiates roughly 65 kilowatts per square metre of surface. By contrast, an oven wall at 200 degrees Celsius, or 473 kelvin, radiates about 2.8 kilowatts per square metre, more than twenty times less, from a temperature only four times higher on the kelvin scale. This nonlinearity is why a broiler browns in two minutes what an oven takes twenty to achieve, and why radiant heating becomes overwhelmingly dominant above about 400 degrees Celsius while being a modest contributor at 150. In a conventional domestic oven at 180 to 220 degrees, radiation from the walls typically supplies somewhere between a third and two-thirds of the total energy reaching food, with the balance from natural convection. Most cooks think of an oven as hot air, which materially understates what is happening. It is why food browns facing the walls, why an oven with a cold glass door cooks unevenly on that side, and why preheating matters: a preheated oven has hot walls that radiate, while an oven that has merely reached air temperature does not. Emissivity, the factor between 0 and 1 in the law, describes how well a surface emits compared to a perfect black body. It matters enormously and is often overlooked. Dark, matt and rough surfaces have emissivity near 0.9 to 0.95; polished metal can be as low as 0.03 to 0.1. Kirchhoff's law states that a good emitter is an equally good absorber at the same wavelength, so the two properties travel together. A dark, dull baking tray absorbs radiant energy strongly and browns bases hard; a shiny aluminium tray reflects most of it and gives pale bottoms. Aluminium foil, shiny on both sides in practical terms, reflects radiant heat and is the standard tool for shielding a browning surface while allowing cooking to continue.

sections.heading: View Factors: The Grill Only Cooks What It Can See
sections.body: Radiation travels in straight lines, and that geometric fact has consequences that neither conduction nor convection share. Engineers handle it with the view factor, sometimes called the configuration or shape factor: the fraction of radiation leaving one surface that arrives directly at another. It depends only on geometry — relative size, distance, orientation — and it is what separates radiant cooking from every other kind. Three geometric rules do most of the work. Radiant intensity from a small source falls with the inverse square of distance, so doubling the gap between food and a grill element quarters the delivered power. Surfaces angled away from the source receive less in proportion to the cosine of the angle between the surface normal and the direction to the source, which is Lambert's cosine law, so a curved item like a chicken receives strongly on the part squarely facing the element and weakly on the flanks. And anything not in direct line of sight receives nothing directly — shadowed regions are heated only by convection and by re-radiation from surrounding surfaces. The practical consequences are immediate and specific. Under a grill, distance is the primary control, not the setting: bringing a tray from 20 centimetres to 10 centimetres roughly quadruples the radiant flux, which is a far more decisive change than adjusting a dial. This is why grilling instructions specify a shelf position and why moving a dish up or down is the correct response to browning too slowly or too fast. It explains why food touching a hot solid surface browns where it touches and steams elsewhere, why a crowded roasting tin gives pale sides where pieces shade one another, and why turning is necessary: rotating a piece changes which surface faces the source. It also explains why a rotisserie produces such even browning, since continuous rotation averages the view factor over the whole surface. It explains the behaviour of enclosures. Inside an oven, food is surrounded by hot walls in every direction, so the total view factor from food to hot surfaces approaches one and radiant heating is nearly uniform — the opposite of the highly directional case under a grill. Opening the door replaces part of that hot enclosure with a cold room, which cuts radiant input as well as letting hot air escape, and is a real reason repeated door-opening slows cooking more than the recovery of air temperature suggests. Finally, it explains barbecue technique. Direct grilling over coals is dominated by radiation with a high view factor and a source near 600 to 700 degrees Celsius. Moving food to the side for indirect cooking removes line of sight almost entirely, leaving convection and reflected radiation from the lid — a completely different cooking mode achieved without changing the fire at all.

sections.heading: Wavelength and Penetration: Not All Radiant Heat Is Alike
sections.body: Radiant heat is not a single substance delivered in different amounts. Its wavelength changes with source temperature, and wavelength determines how deeply it penetrates and what absorbs it — which is why two grills at nominally similar power can behave quite differently. Wien's displacement law gives the peak wavelength of emitted radiation as approximately 2,898 divided by absolute temperature, in micrometres. An oven wall at 473 kelvin peaks near 6.1 micrometres, deep in the far infrared. A glowing electric grill at 1,073 kelvin peaks near 2.7 micrometres, in the mid infrared. Charcoal at about 1,200 kelvin peaks near 2.4 micrometres and emits visibly. A halogen or quartz lamp running at 2,500 to 3,000 kelvin peaks near 1 micrometre, in the near infrared, and appears bright white. Penetration depth follows. Far-infrared radiation is absorbed by water within a fraction of a millimetre, so it heats the surface only and everything below must be reached by conduction. Near-infrared penetrates food to perhaps 1 to 5 millimetres, depositing energy in a thin subsurface layer rather than purely at the face. This is why quartz and halogen grills sear rapidly with a distinctive character, and why they can dry a surface less severely for the same browning, since some energy is delivered below the evaporating face. Microwaves are the extreme case and deserve a note because they are frequently misdescribed as a fourth transport mode. At 2.45 gigahertz, the wavelength is about 12 centimetres and the mechanism is entirely different: the oscillating electric field torques polar water molecules, which rotate and lose energy to their neighbours through friction. This is dielectric heating, and it is genuine volumetric heating rather than transport from a surface. Penetration depth in moist food is roughly 1 to 3 centimetres, so a large item still has a cold core and still relies on conduction to even out. Because ice's molecules are locked in a lattice and rotate poorly, frozen regions absorb far less than liquid water, which is why defrosting is uneven and why a thawed patch runs away and cooks while the ice beside it stays frozen. Surface optical properties matter at these wavelengths too, and not always intuitively. Colour in the visible spectrum is a poor guide to far-infrared behaviour: most non-metallic surfaces, including white ceramic, pale food and even white paint, have emissivity above 0.9 in the far infrared and are effectively black to it. Metals are the genuine exception, reflecting strongly at all infrared wavelengths. So a white ceramic dish absorbs oven radiation nearly as well as a black one, while a shiny metal tray genuinely does not — which corrects a common assumption that pale bakeware is uniformly gentler.

sections.heading: Evaporation: The Sink That Pins a Wet Surface at 100 Degrees
sections.body: Any account of heat transfer that stops at the three modes will mispredict what happens on the surface of real food, because a large fraction of the arriving energy is not raising the temperature at all. It is boiling water off. The latent heat of vaporisation of water is about 2,260 kilojoules per kilogram at 100 degrees Celsius, and around 2,440 at 25 degrees. For comparison, raising a kilogram of water from 0 to 100 degrees takes about 419 kilojoules. Evaporating water therefore costs roughly five and a half times as much energy as heating it across the entire liquid range. Whenever a food surface is wet, energy arriving there is consumed by evaporation, and the surface temperature is clamped near the boiling point of water — around 100 degrees Celsius at sea level, lower at altitude, slightly higher in a salty or sugary solution. This clamp has a specific and important consequence: the Maillard reaction, which produces most savoury browning, runs usefully only above about 140 to 150 degrees Celsius, and caramelisation of sucrose begins around 160. A wet surface cannot reach those temperatures. Browning therefore cannot begin until the surface has dried, and every technique that improves browning is at bottom a technique for drying the surface sooner: patting meat dry, salting in advance and blotting the drawn moisture, using a hot enough pan that the initial water flashes off, not crowding the pan so that escaping vapour can leave, and choosing a fan oven when a dry exterior is wanted. It also explains the temperature plateau familiar to anyone using a probe thermometer during long cooking. In barbecue, a large piece of pork or brisket often stalls for hours somewhere around 65 to 71 degrees Celsius. The dominant explanation, supported by controlled experiments, is evaporative cooling: moisture reaching the surface evaporates as fast as energy arrives, so the whole heat budget goes into latent heat and the internal temperature stops climbing. Wrapping the meat in foil or paper, the technique known as the Texas crutch, suppresses evaporation and the temperature immediately resumes rising. The competing explanation involving connective-tissue changes has largely been ruled out by experiments in which the same stall appears with wet cloth and vanishes with wrapping. The reverse process is equally important. When steam condenses on a cold surface it releases that same enormous latent heat, which is why steaming cooks so fast and why steam burns are so severe. Injecting steam into a bread oven for the first minutes keeps the crust moist and elastic so the loaf can expand, then withdrawing it allows the surface to dry and colour. The same principle explains why a lid transforms a pan: trapped vapour condenses on the food and on the lid, moving energy around rapidly while holding the surface wet, so a covered pan cooks faster and browns less.

sections.heading: A Diagnostic: Working Out Which Mode Is Doing the Work
sections.body: Given an unfamiliar setup, it is usually possible to determine which mechanism dominates in under a minute, and the answer tells you which lever to pull. The reasoning follows a small number of questions asked in order, and the underlying principle is simple: identify the largest thermal resistance in the path from the energy source to the point you care about, because that is the only place an improvement will help. Two orientation facts make the questions easy to answer. First, if the food touches a solid, dense hot object over a meaningful area, conduction almost always dominates at that interface, because solid contact carries far more power than air ever will. Second, if the source is glowing — visibly red, orange or white — radiation dominates, because the fourth-power law has taken over. Once the dominant external mode is known, one further question decides where the bottleneck sits. Compare how fast energy arrives at the surface with how fast it can move inward. For thin items, external delivery is limiting and changing the source works. For thick items the internal conduction is limiting, and the only real levers are time, geometry and lowering the external temperature so the outside survives while the inside catches up.
steps: Ask what physically touches the food. Solid contact over real area means conduction dominates there; a fluid all round means convection; nothing but a line of sight to something glowing means radiation.
Look at the source temperature. Below about 250 degrees Celsius, convection and radiation are comparable in an enclosure. Above about 400, or if the source glows, radiation dominates decisively.

Identify the fluid. Air gives a heat transfer coefficient around 5 to 60; oil 250 to 1,000; boiling water 1,000 to 3,000; condensing steam 5,000 or more. A change of fluid outranks almost any change of temperature.
Ask whether the fluid is moving, and whether the food is crowded. Still fluid and packed trays mean thick boundary layers and slow transfer regardless of the setting.
Check whether the surface is wet. A wet surface is pinned near 100 degrees Celsius and cannot brown, so browning problems are moisture problems before they are heat problems.
Estimate the Biot number roughly as h times half-thickness divided by the food's conductivity of about 0.45. A value well above 1 means the interior lags badly and steep gradients are unavoidable.
Apply the square law to the thickness. Doubling thickness roughly quadruples the time to heat the centre, so compare pieces by thickness before comparing them by weight.
Name the largest resistance in the chain, then change only that. Improving anything else in series with a dominant resistance produces no measurable benefit.

sections.heading: Shifting the Dominant Mode Deliberately
sections.body: Once you can name the dominant mechanism, the useful move is often not to intensify it but to switch to a different one. Most classical techniques are exactly that: a deliberate choice of which mode carries the energy. To increase conduction, increase contact. Press the food down, use a weighted press or a second pan, use a heavier and flatter pan, add a film of oil to fill the microscopic voids, and make sure the food is dry so the contact is metal-to-food rather than metal-to-steam. Preheat the pan thoroughly, because a pan that has reached temperature only at its base still has cold mass that will pull the surface down on contact. Choosing a high-effusivity pan such as cast iron or thick carbon steel keeps the surface temperature up when cold food lands. To increase convection, change the fluid or move it. Switching from air to water multiplies h by about a hundred; switching from water to oil raises the achievable temperature above 100 degrees while keeping a respectable h; switching to condensing steam raises h higher still. Failing a change of fluid, move it: turn on the fan, stir, space food out, use a rack, avoid overfilling a fryer basket, and accept that reducing the load is often faster than raising the temperature. To increase radiation, get closer and expose the surface. Halving the distance to a grill element roughly quadruples the flux. Removing anything that blocks line of sight — a lid, a crowded neighbour, a high-sided tin — has a comparable effect. Choosing dark, matt bakeware raises absorbed radiation substantially over shiny aluminium. Preheating a heavy stone or steel in the oven creates a large hot radiating and conducting surface, which is exactly why pizza cooked on a preheated stone behaves entirely differently from pizza on a cold tray. To reduce a mode, invert each of these. Foil shields reflect radiation away from a browning surface while allowing convection to continue. A lid suppresses evaporation and converts an open roasting environment into a moist, steam-dominated one, which speeds internal heating and prevents browning simultaneously. Raising food on a rack removes conductive contact. Turning off the fan reduces h and softens surface drying. Baking in a water bath caps the surrounding temperature at 100 degrees and buffers it, which is why custards and cheesecakes are cooked that way — the water's enormous heat capacity resists swings and the phase change caps the ceiling. The most useful compound techniques combine modes in sequence rather than at once. The reverse sear cooks a thick steak in a low oven, where mild convection produces a shallow gradient and an even interior, then finishes it in a screaming pan where conduction and radiation build a crust in ninety seconds. Each stage is chosen because a different mechanism is appropriate to a different goal, and attempting both goals with one mechanism is precisely what produces a grey band under a thin crust.

sections.heading: Real Setups Compared: The Same Temperature, Different Results
sections.body: Running several familiar methods through the same framework shows how far apart identically labelled temperatures can be, and makes the abstractions concrete. Boiling at 100 degrees Celsius is convection-dominated, with h around 1,000 to 3,000 because bubbling agitates the liquid vigorously. The temperature ceiling is fixed by the phase change, so the food surface cannot exceed 100 and no browning occurs. Energy delivery is fast but the ceiling is low: excellent for cooking through, useless for crust. Steaming, counterintuitively, delivers energy at least as fast, because condensing steam has an h of 5,000 or more. It is often described as gentler; thermodynamically it is not, and it cooks at a similar rate to boiling while leaching less soluble material into the water. A conventional oven at 200 degrees runs a mixed regime: natural convection with h around 10, plus radiation from the walls contributing a comparable or larger share. Total effective delivery is modest, which is why a roast takes an hour and why the interior has time to equilibrate. Adding a fan lifts h to about 30 and shortens the time by roughly a quarter to a third. Pan frying at 200 degrees is a different world. Conduction through direct metal contact gives an effective transfer coefficient that dwarfs the oven's, so the contact face heats explosively while the top face sits in still room air with h near 5. The gradient across the food is extreme, which is exactly why frying browns quickly and why turning is essential. Deep frying at 180 degrees is convection in oil, h of 250 to 1,000, delivered to the entire surface simultaneously and uniformly. Its distinguishing feature is that escaping moisture from the food creates violent bubbling, which stirs the oil and raises h further, and forms a vapour barrier that keeps oil from soaking in while the food is actively steaming. The crust forms because the surface can exceed 100 degrees once locally dry, while the interior steams at 100. Grilling under a broiler is radiation-dominated, with an element at 700 to 1,000 degrees delivering tens of kilowatts per square metre to the exposed face and essentially nothing to the shadowed one. Distance, not the dial, is the control. Sous vide at 60 degrees is convection in water with a modest temperature difference. Its point is not speed but that the driving temperature difference is small and the target temperature is the water temperature, so the Biot number ceases to matter — the food cannot overshoot, gradients vanish given time, and doneness becomes a function of temperature alone rather than of timing. The general lesson from the comparison is that the number on the dial is the least informative part of a cooking instruction. Two processes at 200 degrees can differ in delivered power by a factor of fifty, purely through the choice of medium and contact, and it is that factor, not the temperature, that determines whether the result is a crust, a steady roast or a slow bake.

sections.heading: Measuring It: What Each Instrument Actually Reads
sections.body: Every practical decision about heat transfer depends on measurement, and the common instruments each measure something slightly different from what the user assumes. A probe thermometer reads the temperature of its own sensing element, which sits at the tip for a thermocouple or thermistor and may extend several centimetres along the stem for a bimetallic dial type. The reading is correct only once the probe has equilibrated with its surroundings, and the probe itself conducts heat along its stem from the hotter exterior, biasing readings upward in a thin item. Placement is the dominant error: in a thick piece the temperature varies by tens of degrees over a couple of centimetres, so a probe a little off centre reads meaningfully high. Insert to the geometric centre of the thickest part, avoid bone and fat pockets, and if unsure push the probe through and withdraw it slowly, watching for the minimum reading, which locates the centre. Response time matters. A fine thermocouple stabilises in one to three seconds; a thick dial probe can take fifteen to thirty. In a fast-moving situation like a thin steak, a slow probe is not merely inconvenient but wrong, because the reading lags a rapidly changing value. An infrared thermometer reads emitted radiation from a surface and infers temperature, which introduces two systematic problems. It measures a spot whose diameter grows with distance, typically in a ratio of about 8 to 1 or 12 to 1, so from 60 centimetres it averages over a patch several centimetres across. And it assumes an emissivity, usually fixed near 0.95. On food, dark pans and most ceramics that assumption is close enough. On shiny metal, with emissivity possibly below 0.1, it is badly wrong and will read far too low while also picking up reflections of other hot objects. Reading a polished pan with an infrared gun is one of the most common measurement errors in a kitchen. A patch of masking tape or a smear of oil gives a high-emissivity target to aim at. An oven thermostat measures air temperature at one point, usually near a wall, and cycles the element around a set point. Actual air temperature typically swings 10 to 20 degrees either side of the setting, and thermostat calibration errors of 10 to 25 degrees are routine. More importantly, it says nothing about wall temperature and therefore nothing about the radiant share, which is why a nominally preheated oven that has only just reached temperature cooks differently from one held for twenty minutes. An independent oven thermometer left in place, and a habit of preheating for longer than the beep suggests, correct most of this. Whatever the instrument, the discipline is the same: know which physical quantity it senses, where it senses it, and how long it needs to settle, because every one of these devices reports its own condition rather than the food's.

sections.heading: Failure Modes and the Mode-Specific Fix
sections.body: Most recurring cooking failures are a single mechanism misapplied, and each has a fix that follows from the mechanism rather than from folklore. Burnt outside, raw inside is a Biot number problem. Energy arrives at the surface far faster than conduction carries it inward, so the surface reaches destruction temperature long before the centre is done. Raising the heat makes it strictly worse. The fixes are to reduce the external temperature and extend the time, to reduce the thickness so the square law works for you, or to split the job into two stages, cooking through gently and browning briefly at the end. Starting from a less cold interior helps: an item taken from the refrigerator has a larger internal deficit to make up while the surface burns. Grey, weeping, unbrowned meat is an evaporation and boundary-layer problem. The surface never dried, so it stayed pinned near 100 degrees and could not reach Maillard temperatures. Causes are a wet surface, a pan that was not hot enough, too much food in the pan so the released moisture could not escape and the pan temperature collapsed, or a pan with low effusivity that lost its surface heat on contact. Dry the food, preheat properly, cook in batches, and use a heavier pan. Pale bottoms on baked goods are a radiation and contact problem. A shiny aluminium tray reflects radiant energy, and an insulated or double-layer tray deliberately reduces conduction. Switch to a dark, matt, heavy tray, or preheat a baking stone or steel and slide the item onto it. Uneven results across an oven shelf are a stratification and view-factor problem. A still oven can run 20 to 30 degrees hotter at the top, and items near a wall receive more radiation than those in the middle. Rotate trays halfway through, swap shelf positions, avoid crowding, and use the fan if the recipe tolerates it. A pan with a stubborn hot centre or cold ring is a contact and conductivity problem: a warped base, or thin stainless without a disc. Test flatness with a straight edge across the base. If the pan is warped, replace it, or move to gas where contact matters less. Food that steams instead of roasting is a moisture and convection problem. Too much food per unit tray area releases more vapour than the oven can carry away, raising local humidity and suppressing drying. Use a larger tray, cook in two batches, raise the temperature, and use a rack for airflow underneath. Finally, carryover overshoot is a stored-energy problem, not a mistake in the cooking. A hot outer shell continues to conduct inward after removal from the heat, and the centre of a large roast can rise 5 to 10 degrees more, a thin steak only 1 to 3. Remove large items below target by an amount proportional to their size, and rest them. Resting is not decorative: it lets the internal gradient flatten, which is why a rested piece is evenly done edge to centre rather than banded.

guides.safetyNote: Hot oil, steam and radiant elements injure faster than hot air. Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius but frying oil commonly runs at 175 to 190, and steam releases about 2,260 kilojoules per kilogram as it condenses on skin, which is why a steam burn is far worse than a splash of boiling water. Never add water to hot oil; never move a pan of oil that has begun to smoke. Keep a well-fitting lid within reach to smother an oil fire and never use water on one. Radiant grills and glass oven doors reach temperatures that burn on contact well after the appliance is switched off, and a metal handle inside an oven conducts heat fast enough to cause a deep burn in under a second. Cooking food to a safe internal temperature is a separate question from heat transfer and should be verified with a probe thermometer, not inferred from time or colour.

guides.title: How Heat Moves in the Kitchen
guides.summary: How conduction, convection, radiation and phase change actually move energy into food, and how those mechanisms explain pans, ovens, frying, browning, resting and every cooking technique built on them.

sections.heading: Cooking Is Heat Transfer With Flavour Attached
sections.body:
Almost every technique a cook learns is a rule of thumb wrapped around a heat transfer problem. Sear the steak before you roast it. Don't crowd the pan. Let the meat rest. Bring the roast to room temperature. Bake bread with steam for the first ten minutes. Reduce a convection oven by twenty degrees. Each of these is a genuine physical insight compressed into an instruction, and each becomes far more useful once the underlying mechanism is visible, because you can then reason about the cases the rule does not cover.

There are only three ways energy moves from a heat source into food, and a fourth process that is not strictly heat transfer but dominates practical cooking. Conduction is the transfer of energy through direct contact between molecules that are touching, atom jostling atom, with no bulk movement of material. Convection is the transfer of energy by the bulk movement of a fluid — air, water, oil, steam — that carries hot material to a cold surface and takes cold material away. Radiation is the transfer of energy as electromagnetic waves, which requires no medium at all and travels at the speed of light. The fourth process is phase change: the absorption or release of very large amounts of energy when a substance melts, boils or condenses at constant temperature.

Every cooking method is a particular blend of these. A pan sear is dominated by conduction from metal to meat. A pot of boiling water is convection carrying heat to the food surface followed by conduction inward. An oven is roughly half radiation from the hot walls and half natural convection from the circulating air, with the ratio shifting toward convection when a fan is running. A grill over coals is overwhelmingly radiation. A microwave oven is none of the three, because it deposits energy directly in the food by exciting water molecules rather than transferring heat from a hotter body.

The reason this matters practically is that the three mechanisms behave differently in ways that show up on the plate. Radiation intensity falls with the fourth power of the source temperature and with the square of the distance, so moving a steak from ten centimetres under a broiler to twenty centimetres cuts the incident energy fourfold. Conduction depends on contact, so a pan that is fractionally warped delivers heat to a fraction of the food. Convection depends on fluid motion, so a crowded pan that stalls airflow and floods itself with steam cannot brown.

Understanding which mechanism dominates a given process tells you which variable to change when the result is wrong. If a roast is pale but cooked through, you have a radiation and surface-drying problem, not a time problem. If a steak is grey to the centre, you have a conduction and thickness problem. If bread is burnt on the bottom and raw in the middle, you have unequal mechanisms acting on the same object. Diagnosis becomes possible instead of guesswork.

sections.heading: Heat Is Not Temperature: The Distinction That Explains Everything
sections.body:
The most common conceptual error in the kitchen is treating heat and temperature as the same thing. They are not, and the difference explains a whole class of otherwise puzzling behaviour.

Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules in a substance — how vigorously they are jiggling. It is an intensive property, meaning it does not depend on how much of the substance you have. A teaspoon of boiling water and a stockpot of boiling water are both at 100 degrees Celsius. Heat is energy in transit from a hotter body to a colder one, measured in joules. It is extensive: the stockpot contains vastly more of it, which is why it will scald you badly and the teaspoon will not.

The bridge between them is specific heat capacity, the energy required to raise one kilogram of a substance by one kelvin. Water is the outlier of everyday materials at 4.18 kilojoules per kilogram per kelvin — it takes more energy to warm than almost anything else you will encounter. Cooking oil is about 2.0, air about 1.0, cast iron 0.46, aluminium 0.90, copper 0.385, and stainless steel about 0.50. Meat, being mostly water, comes in around 3.0 to 3.5 depending on fat content, and fat itself is roughly 2.0.

Run the numbers on a real case. Raising one litre of water from 20 to 100 degrees requires 1 kilogram times 4.18 kilojoules times 80 kelvin, or 334 kilojoules. A domestic electric hob element delivering 2 kilowatts, with perhaps 70 percent of that reaching the pot, supplies 1.4 kilojoules per second, so the theoretical minimum is about 240 seconds — four minutes. Anything longer than that is loss to the room and to the pot itself. Meanwhile raising a 2 kilogram cast iron skillet from 20 to 200 degrees takes 2 times 0.46 times 180, about 166 kilojoules — half as much energy as the litre of water despite the far higher temperature.

This is why a heavy pan takes minutes to preheat and then holds its temperature when cold food lands in it, while a thin one heats in seconds and crashes the moment food arrives. The pan's ability to resist a temperature drop is its thermal mass, the product of its mass and its specific heat, and it is measured in joules per kelvin. That 2 kilogram cast iron skillet has a thermal mass of about 920 joules per kelvin. A 400 gram thin aluminium pan has about 360. Drop a cold 200 gram steak into each and the difference in surface temperature crash is exactly what determines whether you get a crust or grey steamed meat.

Temperature tells you which direction energy will flow and how fast. Total energy content tells you whether the source can sustain that flow. Both matter, and confusing them produces most of the disappointments in home cooking.

sections.heading: Conduction: Fourier's Law and Why Materials Differ So Much
sections.body:
Conduction is energy passing through matter without the matter itself moving. In a metal, most of it is carried by free electrons, which is why good electrical conductors are almost always good thermal conductors. In an insulator or in food, it is carried by lattice vibrations and molecular collisions, which is far less efficient.

The governing relationship was written down by Joseph Fourier in 1822 and is elegantly simple: the rate of heat flow through a slab is proportional to the area, proportional to the temperature difference across it, and inversely proportional to its thickness. In symbols, q equals k times A times the temperature difference divided by the thickness. The constant k is thermal conductivity, measured in watts per metre per kelvin, and it is a property of the material alone.

The spread of values across kitchen materials is enormous and worth memorising in rough terms. Copper is about 400 watts per metre-kelvin. Aluminium is 205 to 237 depending on alloy. Cast iron is 50 to 80. Carbon steel is around 45. Stainless steel — specifically the 18/10 austenitic grades used in cookware — is only about 16, some twenty-five times worse than aluminium. Glass and ceramic are around 1. Water is 0.6. Lean meat is 0.45 to 0.5, and fat about 0.17 to 0.2. Air is 0.026, which is roughly fifteen thousand times worse than copper, and is why every insulator ever made is essentially a device for trapping still air.

Two practical conclusions follow immediately. First, a stainless steel pan used alone is a poor cooking surface, because heat delivered to one spot on the base spreads sideways very slowly and produces hot spots directly over the burner. This is exactly why quality stainless cookware is clad: a core of aluminium or copper, typically 2 to 4 millimetres thick, sandwiched between thin stainless layers that provide the durable, non-reactive cooking surface. The stainless is there for chemistry and wear; the aluminium is there for physics.

Second, food conducts heat badly. With a conductivity around 0.5, meat is closer to plastic than to metal. This is the reason a thick roast takes hours rather than minutes, and it is the reason the temperature inside a cooking joint is never uniform: at any moment there is a steep gradient from a scorching surface to a cool centre, and that gradient is the whole story of doneness.

Fat is a further complication because it conducts less than half as well as lean muscle. A well-marbled steak genuinely cooks more slowly and more evenly than a lean one, and a thick fat cap acts as a real insulating blanket. This is why crackling on a pork joint browns while the meat beneath stays moist, and why scoring the fat both allows rendering and speeds conduction into the meat below.

sections.heading: Thermal Diffusivity and the Square Law of Thickness
sections.body:
Conductivity alone does not tell you how fast a temperature front travels through food, because a material that conducts well but also stores a lot of energy per degree will still warm slowly. The quantity that governs the speed of the front is thermal diffusivity, written alpha, and defined as thermal conductivity divided by the product of density and specific heat capacity. Its units are square metres per second, and it answers the question a cook actually cares about: how quickly does the inside find out what is happening at the outside.

Meat has a thermal diffusivity of roughly 1.4 times ten to the minus seven square metres per second, essentially identical to water, which is unsurprising since meat is about 75 percent water. Copper, by contrast, is about 1.1 times ten to the minus four — nearly a thousand times faster. Fat is around 1.0 times ten to the minus seven, and dry bread crumb, being full of air pockets, is slower still.

The critical consequence is that the characteristic time for heat to penetrate a distance L scales as L squared divided by alpha. The square is everything. Doubling the thickness of a piece of meat does not double the cooking time; it roughly quadruples it. A steak 2 centimetres thick reaching 55 degrees at its centre in 8 minutes implies a 4 centimetre steak needing something near 32 minutes at the same surface conditions. This single relationship explains why weight-based roasting charts — twenty minutes per pound and so on — are so unreliable. Two joints of equal weight but different shapes cook in very different times, because what matters is the shortest distance from surface to centre, not the mass.

The same square law explains the two-stage strategy behind almost all serious meat cookery. If you apply enough surface heat to brown quickly, the surface reaches 150 degrees or more while the centre is still cold, and by the time conduction has carried enough energy to the centre the outer centimetre is overcooked and grey. The solution is to separate the two jobs: bring the interior gently to target with mild heat, where the shallow gradient lets the whole mass approach uniformity, then apply an intense, brief surface treatment that browns before it has time to penetrate. Reverse-searing a steak and finishing a sous-vide roast under a blowtorch or in a screaming pan are both applications of this reasoning.

A useful rule of thumb follows for planning. Heat penetrates moist food at something like 1 centimetre in 8 to 12 minutes at moderate oven temperatures, though the number depends on surface conditions. That means the interior of a thick roast simply cannot be rushed, and a raised oven temperature buys far less time than intuition suggests while costing a great deal in overcooked outer layers.

The corollary in the other direction is that thin things are governed entirely by surface conditions. A crêpe, a thin fish fillet or a scallop has no meaningful interior; whatever happens at the surface happens throughout almost instantly, which is why such foods go from perfect to ruined in seconds.

sections.heading: Convection: Boundary Layers and Why Stirring Works
sections.body:
Convection is heat transfer by a moving fluid, and it is the mechanism at work whenever food sits in air, water, oil or steam. It comes in two varieties. Natural convection is driven by buoyancy alone: fluid touching a hot surface expands, becomes less dense, rises, and is replaced by cooler fluid. Forced convection is driven by a fan, a pump, a stirring spoon or a rolling boil.

The subtlety that makes convection interesting is the boundary layer. Fluid immediately touching a solid surface does not move at all — this is the no-slip condition of fluid mechanics — so there is always a thin, nearly stationary film of fluid clinging to the food. Heat must cross that film by conduction before the bulk fluid can carry it away. The film is therefore the bottleneck, and anything that thins it dramatically increases heat transfer. Stirring, whisking, a rolling boil, a convection fan and simply moving food around a pan all work by thinning the boundary layer.

Engineers bundle all this into a single number, the convective heat transfer coefficient h, measured in watts per square metre per kelvin, and use Newton's law of cooling: the heat flux equals h times the area times the temperature difference. The values differ by orders of magnitude and explain a great deal of kitchen experience. Still air is only 5 to 10. Air blown by an oven fan is 20 to 50. Hot oil at frying temperature is roughly 200 to 1,000. Water below boiling is 500 to 1,500, and vigorously boiling water 2,000 or more. Condensing steam is 5,000 to 15,000, the highest of all common cases.

That table settles several familiar arguments. It is why a domestic oven at 200 degrees will not burn your hand in an instant while 200 degree oil will destroy it: the temperature is the same, the heat flux is a hundred times greater. It is why 100 degree steam scalds far worse than 100 degree water. It is why blanching in a large volume of hard-boiling water cooks vegetables in a fraction of the time that the same water at a bare simmer takes, even though the two are within a degree or two of each other. And it is why a convection oven at 180 degrees cooks roughly as fast as a conventional oven at 200 to 205, which is the origin of the standard advice to reduce the setting by about 20 degrees Celsius or 25 Fahrenheit.

The negative case is equally instructive. Crowding a pan collapses convection. Food released moisture flashes to steam, that steam displaces air, the pan temperature crashes toward 100 degrees because evaporation is consuming energy, and the boundary layer becomes a stagnant blanket of vapour. Nothing browns. Cooking in batches is not fastidiousness; it is a direct manipulation of the convective term.

sections.heading: Radiation: The Fourth-Power Law and the Invisible Half of an Oven
sections.body:
Every object above absolute zero emits electromagnetic radiation, and it does so with an intensity that rises with the fourth power of its absolute temperature. The Stefan-Boltzmann law states that the power radiated per unit area equals the emissivity times the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, 5.67 times ten to the minus eight watts per square metre per kelvin to the fourth, times temperature in kelvin raised to the fourth power. Emissivity ranges from near 1 for dark, matt, rough surfaces to below 0.05 for polished metal.

The fourth power is the crucial fact. Consider an oven wall at 200 degrees Celsius, which is 473 kelvin, against a broiler element glowing at 800 degrees Celsius, or 1,073 kelvin. The ratio of temperatures is 2.27, but the ratio of radiated power is 2.27 to the fourth, about 26. This is why a broiler chars a surface in ninety seconds that an oven would take twenty minutes to colour, and why grilling over glowing coals at 700 to 900 degrees is a fundamentally different process from roasting, not merely a hotter one.

Wien's displacement law tells you what kind of radiation you are dealing with: peak wavelength in micrometres equals about 2,898 divided by the absolute temperature. An oven wall at 473 kelvin peaks at 6.1 micrometres, deep in the far infrared, invisible and absorbed within a fraction of a millimetre of the food surface. A glowing element at 1,100 kelvin peaks near 2.6 micrometres, still infrared but with some visible red. Charcoal at 1,200 kelvin peaks at 2.4 micrometres. In all cooking cases the radiation is absorbed essentially at the surface and must then travel inward by conduction, so radiant heat is a surface treatment, not a penetrating one, despite persistent folklore to the contrary.

Radiation also obeys an inverse square law with distance from a small source and a geometric view factor from an extended one. Doubling the distance from a broiler element to the food cuts the incident flux roughly fourfold. This is the most powerful and most underused control on a domestic grill: the oven rack position matters more than the setting.

Emissivity explains why cookware colour and finish matter more than most people expect. A dark, matt, blackened baking sheet absorbs radiant energy far better than a shiny aluminium one, which reflects it. Bake identical cookies on both in the same oven and the dark sheet browns the bases noticeably faster — often enough to burn them. Conversely, wrapping something in shiny foil deliberately reflects radiation away and slows surface browning, which is exactly what a foil tent over a resting or over-browning roast is doing.

Radiation is also the reason a cast iron pan preheated in a hot oven sears so ferociously. The metal is not only conducting on contact; its whole hot mass is radiating into everything nearby.

sections.heading: Phase Change and Latent Heat: Water's Enormous Energy Bill
sections.body:
When a substance changes state it absorbs or releases a large quantity of energy at constant temperature. This is latent heat, and for water the numbers are exceptional. Melting ice requires 334 kilojoules per kilogram — the same energy that would otherwise raise that water by 80 degrees. Boiling water into steam at 100 degrees requires 2,257 kilojoules per kilogram, roughly five and a half times the energy needed to take the same water from freezing to boiling in the first place.

That figure of 2,257 is one of the most consequential numbers in cooking. It means evaporation is a colossal energy sink. Every gram of water driven off the surface of a roast, a steak, a loaf or a pan of vegetables carries away 2.26 kilojoules. It also means condensation is a colossal energy source: steam condensing on cold food dumps that same 2,257 kilojoules per kilogram into it instantly, which is why a steamer cooks so fast and why a steam burn is far more severe than a scald from liquid water at the same temperature.

Several kitchen behaviours become obvious in this light. A wet surface cannot exceed 100 degrees at ordinary pressure, because any additional energy goes into evaporation rather than into raising the temperature. That is the reason food does not brown while it is visibly wet or while it is steaming: browning chemistry needs temperatures well above 100, and evaporation clamps the surface below that ceiling until the surface actually dries. Patting meat dry before searing is not fussiness; it removes the water that would otherwise consume the pan's energy budget before any crust could form.

The same principle sets the pace of a braise or a stew. Liquid at a bare simmer is at 100 degrees, and no amount of extra flame raises it — the extra energy simply boils water away faster. A furious boil under a braise is wasted fuel and, worse, agitates and shreds the food. This is also why a lid changes everything: it traps evaporating water, condensation returns the latent heat, and the pot reaches temperature far faster while losing far less liquid.

Ice behaves in the mirror image. A frozen roast placed in an oven spends an enormous amount of energy simply melting, during which its temperature does not rise at all, which is why cooking from frozen takes so much longer than the mass difference suggests and why the outside overcooks in the process.

Pressure changes the whole picture because boiling point depends on pressure. At sea level water boils at 100 degrees; the boiling point falls by roughly 1 degree Celsius per 285 metres of altitude, so at 2,000 metres it is about 93 degrees and food genuinely takes longer. A pressure cooker at 15 pounds per square inch above atmospheric raises the boiling point to about 121 degrees, and because reaction rates roughly double per 10 degree rise, that 21 degree lift cuts cooking times by half to two-thirds.

sections.heading: Cookware: Conductivity Against Thermal Mass
sections.body:
A pan has two independent thermal jobs and they pull in different directions. It must spread heat evenly across its base so the food does not scorch over the burner ring, and it must store enough energy to survive contact with cold food without its surface temperature collapsing. The first job is governed by conductivity; the second by thermal mass, which is mass times specific heat. No single material excels at both, which is why cookware is a landscape of compromises rather than a single best answer.

Copper is the champion of evenness. At around 400 watts per metre-kelvin it conducts twice as well as aluminium and twenty-five times as well as stainless steel, and it responds almost instantly to a change in flame — the classic argument for copper in sugar work and delicate sauces, where a burner adjustment must show up in the pan within seconds. Its density gives it decent mass too, but it is expensive, tarnishes, reacts with acids and so must be lined, and it is heavy.

Aluminium is the practical workhorse: about half of copper's conductivity at a fifth of the price and a third of the density. Its low density means a light aluminium pan has little thermal mass, so thickness matters enormously. A 2 millimetre aluminium pan and a 6 millimetre one behave like different tools.

Cast iron has poor conductivity for a metal — 50 to 80, less than a fifth of aluminium — so it genuinely does develop hot spots over a burner and needs a longer preheat with occasional rotation. What it has instead is enormous thermal mass from sheer thickness and density. A 2 kilogram skillet at 220 degrees holds something like 180 kilojoules above room temperature, so a cold steak barely dents it. That is precisely the property a hard sear needs.

Carbon steel is the compromise: thinner and lighter than cast iron, similar conductivity, less mass but faster response, and it is why professional kitchens use it for everything that must be picked up and moved.

Stainless steel alone is a poor conductor and is used almost exclusively as a cladding layer. Tri-ply and five-ply constructions place 2 to 4 millimetres of aluminium or a copper core between stainless faces, buying the conductivity of the core with the durability, non-reactivity and induction compatibility of the surface. A disc-bottom pan puts the conductive slug only on the base, which works for boiling but leaves the walls poor conductors — visible as a scorch ring where a sauce climbs the side.

Induction hobs change the equation again. They generate eddy currents directly in a ferromagnetic pan base, so the pan is the heating element. Efficiency reaches 85 to 90 percent against roughly 40 percent for gas, response is nearly instantaneous, and the kitchen stays cooler — but the pan must be magnetic, and heat is deposited only where the coil sits.

sections.heading: The Oven Is a Liar: Air, Walls, Water Vapour and Thermal Mass
sections.body:
An oven dial is a request, not a measurement. Domestic ovens control temperature by switching a heating element on and off around a set point, and the resulting swing is typically plus or minus 10 to 15 degrees Celsius, sometimes far worse. Independent testing routinely finds domestic ovens running 10 to 25 degrees away from their dial setting, and the offset often varies with the set point rather than being a fixed error. An inexpensive oven thermometer left permanently on the middle shelf is the single most cost-effective instrument in a kitchen.

More importantly, the air temperature is not what cooks the food. Air has a specific heat of 1 kilojoule per kilogram-kelvin and a density around 0.75 kilograms per cubic metre at 200 degrees, so the entire air volume of a 50 litre oven holds only about 7 kilojoules above room temperature — less energy than is needed to warm a single egg. What actually delivers energy is the radiation from the hot walls, floor, roof and racks, plus natural convection currents, plus conduction from whatever the food is sitting on. Opening the door dumps the air almost instantly but barely touches the walls, which is why an oven recovers its cooking power far faster than a thermometer suggests.

That thermal mass in the walls, and especially in a baking stone or steel, is why professional bread baking depends on preheated masonry. A 1 centimetre steel plate weighing 8 kilograms holds roughly 8 times 0.5 times 200, about 800 kilojoules above room temperature, and it delivers that energy to a loaf's base by direct conduction at a rate no air can match. This is the oven spring mechanism: rapid basal heat drives rapid steam expansion in the dough before the crust sets.

Humidity is the other hidden variable. Moist air transfers heat much better than dry air and, crucially, condensing water vapour dumps latent heat onto a cooler surface. A steam-injected oven in the first ten minutes of a bread bake keeps the crust flexible and gelatinises the surface starch, producing gloss and a thin, crisp shell; after that steam must go, because a wet surface cannot brown. In the other direction, a dry oven pulls moisture from a roast and produces the evaporative cooling that keeps the surface near 100 degrees until it dries.

A fan-assisted or true convection oven raises the convective coefficient from roughly 5 to 10 up to 20 to 50 watts per square metre-kelvin, and also destroys the temperature stratification that leaves the top shelf 20 degrees hotter than the bottom in a still oven. The standard compensation is to reduce the set temperature by about 20 degrees Celsius, or to cut the time by roughly a quarter, but not both. Fan ovens also accelerate surface drying, which helps roast potatoes and harms delicate custards and cakes with a wet set.

sections.heading: Frying: Oil as a Heat Transfer Fluid
sections.body:
Frying is often described as cooking in fat, but from a heat transfer point of view oil is simply a fluid that can exceed 100 degrees Celsius without boiling. That is its whole advantage. Water clamps a surface at 100; oil at 180 delivers the surface temperatures that browning chemistry requires while still surrounding the food and conducting evenly into every crevice.

The convective coefficient of hot oil sits around 200 to 1,000 watts per square metre-kelvin, an order of magnitude above hot air and an order below condensing steam. Combined with a working temperature of 160 to 190 degrees, this makes deep frying one of the fastest cooking methods available. A chip 1 centimetre thick reaches doneness in three to five minutes; the same chip in a 190 degree oven takes half an hour.

What actually happens when food enters oil is a vigorous, structured process. The food's surface water flashes to steam and escapes upward — this is the bubbling, and it is water leaving, not oil entering. That outward flow of steam physically excludes oil from the interior, which is why properly fried food at the correct temperature absorbs surprisingly little fat. Oil uptake happens mostly during cooling, as the food's interior contracts and draws in whatever is clinging to the surface, which is why draining immediately and thoroughly matters more than any other single anti-greasiness measure.

Temperature control is therefore about maintaining the steam barrier. If the oil is too cool, say below 150 degrees, steam generation is feeble, the barrier is weak, oil soaks in, and the result is heavy and pale. If the food is added in too great a quantity, the oil temperature crashes for exactly the same reason a crowded pan fails: the energy going into 2,257 kilojoules per kilogram of evaporation is enormous. A useful discipline is to add no more food than will drop the oil by 15 to 20 degrees, and to let it recover between batches.

Oil breaks down with use. Repeated heating hydrolyses triglycerides into free fatty acids and polymerises them, lowering the smoke point, darkening the oil, and increasing foaming. Fresh refined oils have smoke points from about 200 degrees for many neutral seed oils to 230 or more for refined avocado and rice bran; unrefined oils, including extra virgin olive oil at roughly 160 to 190 depending on quality, are unsuited to high-temperature deep frying. Oil that foams persistently, smells acrid, darkens sharply or smokes below normal working temperature should be discarded.

The Leidenfrost effect is the related phenomenon in dry pans. Above roughly 190 to 200 degrees on a steel surface, a water droplet does not spread and boil but instead levitates on a cushion of its own vapour and skitters about for many seconds. The vapour cushion is an insulator, so heat transfer actually falls. The old test of flicking water into a pan works because a droplet that skitters tells you the surface is above the Leidenfrost point and ready for searing, while one that spreads and hisses tells you it is not yet hot enough.

sections.heading: Browning as a Heat Transfer Problem
sections.body:
Browning is chemistry, but whether it happens is almost entirely a heat transfer question, because the reactions concerned have steep temperature thresholds that a wet surface can never reach.

The Maillard reaction, described by the French physician and chemist Louis-Camille Maillard in 1912, is a cascade beginning with the condensation of a reducing sugar with an amino group from a protein or free amino acid. Through the Amadori rearrangement and hundreds of subsequent steps it produces the pyrazines, furans, thiophenes and melanoidins responsible for the aroma of roast meat, toast, coffee and chocolate. It proceeds slowly at 100 degrees, becomes cook-relevant above roughly 140 degrees, and is rapid above 155. Caramelisation is a distinct process involving sugar alone, requiring no amino group, and starts around 110 degrees for fructose, 160 for glucose and sucrose, and about 180 for maltose.

The practical implication is stark. A wet surface sits at 100 degrees because evaporation consumes every extra joule. Nothing browns until the surface actually dries, and every joule spent evaporating surface water is a joule not spent raising surface temperature. This is why the entire craft of getting a crust reduces to managing surface moisture: patting dry, salting in advance so surface water is drawn out and reabsorbed, air-drying a duck or a pork belly uncovered in the refrigerator overnight, dusting with starch, and refusing to crowd the pan.

It also explains why the sequence of energy delivery matters more than the total. A pan hot enough to sear delivers energy faster than the surface can lose it to evaporation, so the surface dries and climbs past 150 within seconds. A pan at moderate heat delivers energy at roughly the rate evaporation removes it, so the surface hovers near 100 indefinitely and the meat greys and steams.

The persistent claim that searing seals in juices is false, and has been known to be false since Harold McGee's careful demolition of it in the 1980s; controlled experiments show seared meat loses slightly more moisture, not less. Searing is worth doing for flavour and texture, which are ample reasons, but not for moisture retention.

Several accelerants exist. Alkalinity speeds the Maillard reaction sharply, which is why a light dusting of baking soda on onions dramatically shortens caramelising time and why pretzels are dipped in lye.
