The useful habit is not to pick one mode but to ask, for any given setup, which one is currently doing most of the work, because that identifies which control will actually change the outcome.

sections.heading: Grilling Over Coals: Managing a Radiant Bed
sections.body: A charcoal grill is a radiant appliance whose source temperature you cannot dial and whose distance and geometry you must therefore manage instead. Lump hardwood charcoal and briquettes both burn, once flaming has ceased and the surface has ashed grey, at bed temperatures of roughly 700 to 1000 C, with lump running hotter and briquettes more even and longer. At 900 C a bed radiates on the order of 100 kilowatts per square metre at its surface, which is why a hand held five centimetres above cannot stay there for two seconds. The single most useful control is bed arrangement, because it sets both source area and the distribution of view factors across the grate. A two-zone fire, with all the coals banked under one half of the grill and none under the other, gives you a searing zone and a genuine radiant shadow where food receives perhaps a tenth of the flux and finishes gently by convection and lid re-radiation. This one arrangement solves the commonest grilling failure, in which a thick chop chars long before its centre reaches temperature. Sear over the coals for the crust, then move to the shadow, close the lid, and let conduction carry heat inward at its own slow pace. Grate height is the other control and it acts sharply. Doubling the gap between coals and food from five to ten centimetres reduces delivered flux by well over half for a typical bed width, because both the view factor drops and the intervening air absorbs a little. Grills with adjustable grates, like Argentine parrillas with their crank-driven grills or Japanese shichirin, treat height as the primary throttle, and this is a more responsive control than fuel adjustment because it takes effect in a second rather than in ten minutes. Ash is not incidental. A layer of white ash on a coal is an insulating, lower-temperature outer skin, and it can drop the effective radiating temperature by 100 C or more, cutting output by roughly a third. Tapping or fanning the bed knocks ash off and exposes incandescent carbon, which is the mechanism behind the sudden surge of heat every griller has felt after a few waves of a fan. Airflow works the same way from below, which is why bottom vents control intensity and top vents control it more slowly by throttling draft. Finally, most of a coal fire's visible flame contributes far less than it appears. Yellow flames from dripping fat are luminous soot particles that do radiate, but they also deposit acrid soot and polycyclic aromatic compounds on the food. Clean, ashed-over coals with no flame are the target state for good grilling, and any sustained flame usually means fat is burning rather than fuel.

sections.heading: Broilers, Salamanders and Overhead Radiant Cooking
sections.body: A broiler, called a grill in British usage, is a radiant source mounted above the food, and the inversion of geometry changes its behaviour in ways that matter. Because heat rises, an overhead element gets essentially no help from convection: the hot air it creates flows away upward, so almost all of the cooking is radiant. That makes the broiler the purest radiant tool in a domestic kitchen and the most sensitive to distance. Element temperatures vary by type. An electric sheathed element glows dull red at roughly 700 to 900 C. A gas broiler burner heats a ceramic or steel plate to 700 to 1000 C. A commercial infrared salamander uses a ceramic burner face that reaches 900 to 1000 C and comes to full output in around 30 seconds, against several minutes for a metal-sheathed electric element. Cheap domestic broilers cycle on and off on a thermostat, so their average output is much lower than their peak, and this cycling is responsible for the maddening experience of a cheese topping that will not brown: the element is dark half the time. Leaving the oven door ajar on many electric ovens defeats the thermostat and keeps the element continuously on, which is why manuals for some models actually instruct you to do it. Rack position is the throttle, and its effect is severe. Moving food from 15 centimetres below the element to 7 centimetres typically more than doubles the flux, turning a five-minute browning into a ninety-second one. The professional rule of thumb is that thin items that need only colour, such as gratins, cheese toppings, glazed fish fillets and crème brûlée sugar, go close, while anything more than about two centimetres thick goes far, so conduction has time to keep up with surface browning. Broiling has three characteristic pathologies. The first is the shadow: raised edges, a bone, or the rim of a dish cast a genuine shadow and the food beneath stays pale, so rotating the pan halfway is not superstition. The second is uneven element coverage; most domestic broilers are hot in the centre and weak at the corners, and the fix is to move food rather than wait. The third is that wet surfaces will not brown, because evaporating water pins the surface near 100 C by consuming about 2260 kilojoules per kilogram as latent heat. Until the surface film has gone, essentially all arriving energy goes into boiling water rather than raising temperature, and no browning chemistry can begin. Blotting a fillet dry with paper towel before broiling saves more time than any adjustment of the dial. Foil is the broiler's precision instrument. A loose tent of bright foil over one part of a roast reflects nearly all incident infrared while allowing hot air past, so it stops surface browning almost completely without stopping the cooking underneath.

sections.heading: Ovens as Radiant Cavities: Walls, Pans and Position
sections.body: A conventional oven is usually described as hot air, but that description misses most of what is happening. An oven is a closed cavity whose walls, floor, ceiling and racks are all at roughly the set temperature, and every one of those surfaces radiates at the food. Because air is nearly transparent in the infrared and has very low heat capacity, the walls do a large share of the work. At a 180 C setting, radiation typically supplies a third to a half of the total energy reaching food; at 250 C, closer to two-thirds, because of the fourth-power scaling. This explains a set of observations that seem inexplicable if you think only about air temperature. A dark, matte, heavy baking sheet browns cookie bottoms far harder than a shiny aluminium one, because its emissivity is around 0.9 against 0.1 or lower for bright aluminium, and because its mass stores energy to dump into the dough on contact. Glass and ceramic dishes brown differently from metal ones: glass is nearly opaque in the far infrared and has high emissivity, so a Pyrex dish delivers strong radiant heat to its contents while conducting slowly, which is why pie fillings set well but crusts sometimes stay pale. A pan placed on the bottom rack sits close to the floor and to the lower element, receiving markedly more radiant flux from below than one in the middle, which is the physical reason for the standard advice to bake bread low and delicate cakes centrally. Preheating is not about the air, which reaches temperature in a couple of minutes. It is about the walls, the racks and any stone or steel, which take fifteen minutes to an hour depending on mass. An oven that beeps ready after eight minutes has hot air and cool walls, and food put in at that point receives perhaps half the radiant flux it will receive twenty minutes later. Bakers who preheat a baking stone or a thick steel plate for 45 to 60 minutes are deliberately building a high-emissivity thermal reservoir that both conducts fiercely into the loaf's base and radiates upward from the hearth. Convection fans complicate this usefully. A fan does not increase radiation, it increases the convective share, and because forced air also strips away the humid boundary layer clinging to food, surfaces dry faster and therefore begin browning earlier. That is why fan-baked pastry crisps better even at a lower set temperature. Conversely, a crowded oven full of wet food raises humidity, suppresses evaporation, and can leave everything pale despite a correct thermostat reading. Steam injection in bread baking exploits this deliberately: steam for the first ten minutes keeps the crust supple for oven spring, then venting lets radiation take over and set the crust.

sections.heading: Wood-Fired Ovens, Tandoors and Masonry Radiance
sections.body: The wood-fired dome oven, the Indian and Central Asian tandoor, the Middle Eastern taboon and the traditional bread oven are all the same invention: a heavy mass of refractory material charged with heat by a fire, then used as a radiant cavity long after the fire is out or pushed aside. Their performance comes from three properties of masonry. It stores large amounts of energy, roughly 800 to 1000 joules per kilogram per kelvin for firebrick with densities near 2000 kilograms per cubic metre. It has high emissivity, typically 0.85 to 0.95. And a dome shape gives almost every point on the hearth a very high view factor of hot surface, approaching unity, so food is bathed from every direction. A Neapolitan pizza oven is the extreme case. The dome is fired to 430 to 500 C while the floor sits somewhat cooler, typically 380 to 450 C, with a small live flame maintained at one side. A pizza cooks in 60 to 90 seconds because three mechanisms run at once and at maximum: fierce conduction from the floor into the base, intense downward radiation from the dome and the flame onto the top, and convective flow of very hot air. The verification is simple, since a pizza cooked on the same floor in an oven whose dome has cooled will have a burnt base and a raw top. It is the dome's radiation, not the floor, that cooks the surface of the toppings. The tandoor turns this geometry on its side. A clay cylinder is fired with charcoal or wood at its base to wall temperatures of 350 to 480 C. Bread is slapped onto the vertical wall and cooks by conduction from the clay on one face and radiation from the opposite wall and the coals on the other, in 60 to 120 seconds. Skewered meat hangs vertically in the cavity, receiving radiation from all around plus the strong upward radiant column from the coals, which is why tandoori chicken acquires char marks without ever touching a surface. Managing a masonry oven is entirely about reading falling temperature and using the cascade. A bread oven fired to 400 C is swept, loaded with pizza or flatbread at 400 to 450 C, then bread at 250 to 280 C an hour later, then roasts and gratins at 200 C, then slow-braised beans and stocks overnight at 120 C, then meringues and drying herbs at 60 C the following morning. That sequence is not thrift, it is the only sane way to use a store of heat that can only ever decline. An infrared thermometer aimed at the floor and the dome, and a scattering of flour that browns in ten seconds at pizza temperature, are the two field measurements that matter.

sections.heading: Spit-Roasting, Reflector Ovens and Cooking Beside a Fire
sections.body: Before ovens were common, most large-scale roasting in Europe was done beside a fire rather than over it, and the technique is a masterclass in radiant control that modern cooks have largely forgotten. A joint hung or spitted vertically in front of a tall fire receives radiation on one face while dripping fat falls to a pan on the floor rather than into the flames, which eliminates flare-ups and sooty deposits entirely. Rotation solves the one-sided-cooking problem: turning the spit at roughly two to six revolutions per minute means no point on the surface is exposed long enough to burn, while the surface layer as a whole climbs steadily. The rotation also constantly redistributes melted fat over the surface, self-basting the meat, which both conducts heat and raises surface emissivity as it browns. The physics of why rotation works is worth spelling out. Surface temperature responds to radiant flux with a time constant of a few seconds to a few tens of seconds, set by the thermal diffusivity of the meat and the depth of the heated layer. If the exposure interval is short compared with that constant, the surface never reaches the peak temperature it would settle at under continuous exposure, and instead settles near a time-averaged value. A spit turning once every fifteen seconds therefore lets you place meat far closer to a fierce fire than you ever could statically, accelerating cooking without charring. This is exactly the same principle that lets a rotisserie chicken sit 15 centimetres from a burner that would incinerate it if stationary. The reflector oven, sometimes called a tin kitchen or a Dutch reflector, exploits emissivity in the opposite direction. It is a polished metal box, open on the fire side, with the food on a rack or spit inside. The bright interior has an emissivity around 0.05, so it absorbs almost nothing and instead bounces infrared repeatedly onto the food from the back, top and bottom. In effect it raises the food's view factor of the fire from perhaps 0.3 to close to 0.8 without any extra fuel. A reflector oven will roast a chicken in about an hour beside a modest campfire that would take three hours to do the same job unaided. Keeping the reflecting surfaces clean is not cosmetic; a soot-blackened reflector has emissivity near 0.9 and simply absorbs the heat itself, and the oven stops working. The same logic scales down to a foil windbreak behind a camp stove, a sheet of foil tucked behind a roasting rack, or a stone wall built behind a cooking fire. Any reflective or hot surface placed to fill more of the food's view increases the delivered flux. This is one of the highest-return, lowest-cost interventions available in fuel-scarce cooking, and it works identically indoors and out.

sections.heading: Browning Chemistry: Why Radiant Heat Tastes Different
sections.body: The reason cooks chase radiant heat is not speed, it is flavour, and the flavour comes from two families of reaction that need conditions radiant heat is uniquely good at producing: a hot, dry surface with a steep gradient behind it. The Maillard reaction, described by the French physician Louis-Camille Maillard in 1912, is a cascade beginning when the carbonyl group of a reducing sugar condenses with the amino group of an amino acid. The initial product rearranges through the Amadori pathway, then fragments and recombines into hundreds of compounds, including pyrazines that smell roasted and nutty, furans that smell caramel-like, and thiophenes and thiazoles that give meat its meatiness, ending in brown nitrogenous polymers called melanoidins. It runs perceptibly from about 120 C, accelerates sharply above 140 C, and is essentially instantaneous above about 170 C. Caramelisation, the thermal decomposition of sugars alone without amino acids, needs higher temperatures: fructose from about 110 C, glucose about 160 C, sucrose about 170 C. Both are strongly suppressed by water, because while free water remains, evaporation holds the surface near 100 C. This is precisely why radiant heat is the browning tool of choice. It delivers energy fast enough to drive off the surface film and then keep pushing the dried layer up past 150 C, while the food's own poor thermal conductivity keeps the interior far cooler. A steak under an intense broiler can have a surface at 180 C, a layer three millimetres down at 70 C, and a centre at 50 C, all at the same instant. That gradient is the entire point: crust and juiciness simultaneously, which is impossible if you heat the whole thing uniformly. Radiant browning also has a distinct flavour signature compared with pan searing, and there are two reasons. Fat rendering out and falling onto a hot surface below vaporises and partially pyrolyses, sending aldehydes and other volatiles back up onto the food; this smoke, at modest levels, is a large part of what people mean by grilled flavour. And because a radiant crust forms in air rather than in a puddle of fat, it dries more thoroughly and develops a crisper, less greasy texture. The costs deserve equal honesty. Above roughly 200 C surface temperature, amino acids and creatine in muscle form heterocyclic aromatic amines, and incomplete combustion of dripping fat forms polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons which deposit on the food. Both classes include compounds classified as probable human carcinogens. Practical mitigations that measurably reduce them are avoiding direct flame contact, trimming fat, using a two-zone fire, marinating in acidic or herb-rich mixtures, briefly precooking thick items, and discarding heavily blackened material rather than eating it. None of this requires giving up grilling; it requires keeping the crust brown rather than black, which is also where the flavour is best.

sections.heading: Measuring and Calibrating Radiant Heat in a Real Kitchen
sections.body: Radiant intensity is invisible and no domestic appliance reports it, so cooks need practical proxies. Three tools cover almost every case, and each has a specific failure mode worth knowing before you trust it.
ingredients: An infrared thermometer with an adjustable emissivity setting and a distance-to-spot ratio of at least 8:1, sold widely for 20 to 60 units of currency; set emissivity to 0.95 for food, brick, ceramic and soot, and understand that it reads bare shiny metal wildly wrong.

An instant-read probe thermometer accurate to plus or minus 0.5 C with a thin tip and a response time under four seconds; this is the only instrument that tells you whether food is safe, since surface colour never does.
An oven thermometer of the dial or probe type left permanently inside the cavity, because domestic oven thermostats commonly read 10 to 25 C away from truth and drift with age.
A sheet of plain white bread or a tablespoon of ordinary flour as a zero-cost pyrometric indicator for masonry ovens and grills.
Heavy dry leather or aramid gloves and long tongs, since every calibration procedure involves putting a hand where a hand does not belong.
steps: Calibrate the probe first. Fill a glass with crushed ice, top with cold water, stir, wait two minutes, and insert the probe without touching glass or ice; it must read 0 C plus or minus 1 C. If it has an adjustment nut or offset function, correct it now, because every later measurement inherits this error.

Measure the source, not the air. Aim the infrared thermometer at the charcoal bed, the broiler element face, the oven floor or the dome, from a distance that keeps the measured spot smaller than the target; at a 10:1 ratio and 50 centimetres, the spot is 5 centimetres across.

Perform the hand test as a cross-check and to build calibrated intuition. Hold an open palm at the height the food will sit. Forced away in 1 to 2 seconds means roughly 260 C or above and counts as high; 3 to 4 seconds is about 200 to 230 C, medium-high; 5 to 7 seconds is about 175 to 200 C, medium; 8 to 10 seconds is low. Stop the instant it hurts.

For a masonry oven, sweep the hearth clean and scatter a pinch of flour. Blackening within 3 to 5 seconds indicates pizza temperature above about 400 C; browning in 10 to 20 seconds indicates roughly 300 to 350 C; browning slowly over a minute indicates bread temperature near 250 C.

Map the appliance once and write the result down. Cover a rack with slices of white bread edge to edge, run the broiler or oven at a fixed setting until the fastest slice just browns, then photograph the tray. That pattern is a permanent map of your appliance's hot spots.
Re-test after any change of pan, rack position or fuel. A bright pan swapped for a dark one invalidates the map for that dish.

sections.heading: Modern Infrared Equipment: Ceramic, Quartz, Halogen and What Microwaves Are Not
sections.body: Purpose-built infrared appliances have spread through professional and domestic kitchens since the 1980s, and they differ chiefly in their source temperature, which sets both their spectrum and their responsiveness. Ceramic infrared burners, the type used in commercial salamanders and in the sear stations of premium gas grills, burn gas within a porous ceramic tile whose face reaches 900 to 1000 C. The tile has emissivity near 0.9 and reaches full output in about 30 seconds, against several minutes for a sheathed metal element. Because the flame is held inside the ceramic matrix rather than licking free, combustion is near complete, there is little visible flame, and the burner is largely immune to being blown out. Grill manufacturers market these as producing 800 C searing, which is approximately honest about the tile face and misleading about what the food surface reaches, which is still limited by evaporation and conduction to something under 250 C. Quartz and halogen elements run hotter still. A tungsten-halogen lamp filament sits around 2400 to 2900 K, putting its peak emission near 1.0 to 1.2 micrometres in the near infrared, with substantial visible output, which is why they glow blinding white. Near-infrared penetrates a millimetre or two into moist food rather than being stopped at the surface, so halogen sources heat a thin subsurface layer directly and can brown very fast. They also switch on and off in milliseconds, which makes them controllable in ways a thermal mass never is. This is the technology behind halogen countertop ovens and certain high-end conveyor toasters. It is worth stating plainly what microwaves are, because the marketing term infrared oven invites confusion. Microwave ovens operate at 2.45 gigahertz, a wavelength of about 12.2 centimetres, which is not infrared at all and not thermal radiation in the Planck sense; it is a coherent field generated by a magnetron that drives dipole rotation in water molecules. Penetration depth is roughly 1 to 3 centimetres in moist food, orders of magnitude greater than infrared, so microwaves genuinely do heat a volume rather than a surface. That is exactly why they do not brown: no surface layer gets appreciably hotter than the interior, and water pins everything near 100 C. Combination ovens that add a grill element or a halogen lamp exist precisely to supply the browning that microwaves cannot. Induction, similarly, is not radiant. It induces eddy currents directly in ferromagnetic cookware using a magnetic field near 20 to 50 kilohertz, so the pan is the heater and everything downstream is ordinary conduction. Understanding which of these an appliance actually uses tells you immediately whether foil will shield it, whether distance matters, and whether it can brown. A simple test settles most cases: if a sheet of bright foil placed between source and food stops the cooking, the appliance is radiant.

sections.heading: Solar Cooking and Off-Grid Radiant Technique
sections.body: Solar cooking is the purest possible expression of radiant cooking, and it is genuinely useful wherever fuel is scarce, expensive or dangerous to gather. The sun delivers roughly 1000 watts per square metre at the Earth's surface under clear midday conditions, falling to 300 to 600 under haze and near zero under heavy overcast. That figure sets both the promise and the hard limit: a cooker with a one square metre aperture and 60 percent overall efficiency has about 600 watts to work with, comparable to a small electric hob ring but entirely dependent on weather and time of day. Three designs cover the field. The box cooker is an insulated container with a transparent glazed lid and reflective flaps. It works by the greenhouse effect: glass and most clear plastics transmit visible and near-infrared sunlight but are largely opaque to the far infrared that the hot interior re-emits, so energy enters and struggles to leave. A well-built box cooker with a single glazing reaches 120 to 150 C and cooks like a slow oven, taking two to four hours for a pot of beans or rice. Interiors are painted matte black to raise absorptivity above 0.95, and pots should be black, thin and lidded for the same reason. The panel cooker, of which the CooKit designed by Solar Cookers International in 1994 is the archetype, is a folded reflective sheet that concentrates sunlight onto a dark pot sealed inside a clear heat-resistant bag; it is cheap, folds flat, and reaches 100 to 120 C. The parabolic cooker focuses sunlight to a point and can put a pot at 200 C or above, genuinely frying and searing, but it must be re-aimed every fifteen to twenty minutes as the sun moves and its focus is dangerous, capable of igniting wood and causing instant eye injury from reflected glare. Dark glasses and never leaving a focused parabola unattended are non-negotiable. The technique differences from fire cooking are consistent. Start early, because a solar cooker must be loaded by mid-morning to finish by mid-afternoon. Cut food small to shorten conduction distances. Use minimal added water, since there is no excess power to boil it off. Choose dark, thin-walled, lidded pots, and never shiny aluminium ones, which reflect the very energy you are trying to capture. Expect that food will not brown in a box cooker, because 150 C surfaces sitting in humid air cannot reach Maillard conditions; solar cooking excels at stewing, steaming, baking bread and pasteurising water, and is poor at roasting and searing. Water pasteurisation at 65 C held for six minutes is one of its highest-value uses, and a wax-pellet water pasteurisation indicator confirms it has been reached.

sections.heading: Failure Modes and How to Diagnose Them
sections.body: Radiant cooking fails in a small number of recognisable ways, and almost all of them trace back to one of four variables: source temperature, distance, surface moisture, and food thickness. Learning to read the symptom back to the cause turns a ruined dinner into a corrected technique. Black outside, raw inside is the signature failure, and it means the surface received energy faster than conduction could carry it inward. Meat's thermal diffusivity means heat advances roughly one centimetre in ten to fifteen minutes, so a five centimetre thick roast physically cannot be cooked through in the eight minutes it takes to blacken. The fix is never a hotter fire; it is more distance, a two-zone arrangement, a lower rack, rotation, or splitting the job into a gentle phase and a brief searing phase. The reverse-sear method, in which meat is brought to within 10 C of its target in a 110 C oven and then given 60 to 90 seconds a side over intense radiant heat, exists entirely to defeat this failure. Pale and stubbornly grey means one of three things. The surface is still wet, and evaporation is pinning it near 100 C, in which case blot it dry and wait for the sizzle to change pitch. The source is cooler than it looks, most often ashed-over coals or a thermostat-cycling broiler element. Or the food is too far away, and the view factor has collapsed. Test by moving the item five centimetres closer for one minute; if nothing changes, distance was not the problem. Uneven, patchy browning almost always means shadowing or an uneven source. Rotate the food 180 degrees halfway and move items between the centre and edges of the appliance. If a specific corner is always pale, that is a permanent property of the equipment, not of the dish. Flare-ups are burning fat, not burning fuel, and they deposit soot and acrid off-flavours within seconds. Move the food off the flame immediately rather than closing vents and hoping. Trim heavy fat caps, use a drip barrier, or move to indirect heat. Never spray water onto a fat flare on a grill; it scatters burning grease. A bitter, sooty, ashtray flavour is deposited soot from incomplete combustion, most often from resinous or unseasoned wood, lighter fluid residue, or a smouldering fat fire. Sound charcoal fully ashed over produces almost no visible smoke, and any sustained yellow flame or dense smoke means something is wrong. Finally, surface temperatures that overshoot cause acrolein and other harsh pyrolysis products from fats past their smoke point: butter around 150 C, extra-virgin olive oil 160 to 190 C, refined sunflower or peanut oil 225 to 232 C, refined avocado oil around 270 C. Under intense radiant heat, choose the high smoke point oils or none at all.

sections.heading: Limits, Open Questions and Building Real Skill
sections.body: Radiant heat is powerful but it is not universal, and being clear about what it cannot do prevents a great deal of wasted effort. It cannot cook thick items quickly, because the rate-limiting step is conduction through the food and no amount of surface power changes food's thermal diffusivity. It cannot reach into cavities, folds or the shadowed side of anything, so a stuffed bird or a tightly packed tray will always need convection or time. It is poor at gentle, even cooking, which is why custards, delicate fish and most braises belong in water baths or covered pots. And it is intrinsically hard to meter, since no appliance reports flux and the same dial setting means different things as an element ages, a fuel bed matures or a stone loses charge. Some genuinely uncertain areas deserve honest labelling. The exact division of energy between radiation and convection in a domestic oven varies substantially between models, and the commonly quoted figures should be treated as ranges rather than constants. Claims that particular grills sear better because of infrared specifically are frequently marketing rather than measurement, since what actually differs is total flux, evenness and preheat speed. The health arithmetic of grilled meat is real but its magnitude is debated: heterocyclic amines and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons are undeniably formed and are classified as probable carcinogens, but the size of the risk at ordinary household consumption is not settled, and sensible mitigation rather than avoidance is the defensible position. Similarly, the popular claim that searing seals in juices was disproved decades ago; searing produces flavour, not moisture retention, and seared meat can actually lose slightly more moisture. Building skill is mostly a matter of deliberate, recorded experiment on your own equipment. Take one variable at a time. Cook the same item at three rack heights and note the times. Compare a dark pan with a bright one side by side in the same oven. Time how long a scattering of flour takes to brown on your grill grate at each vent setting, and write it on the lid with a marker. Photograph a bread-slice map of your broiler. These take an hour in total and permanently replace guesswork with numbers for the specific appliances in front of you, which no general advice can supply. The unifying idea is simple enough to carry anywhere. Radiant cooking is the art of applying very high power to a very thin layer while the interior lags behind, and every control you have is really a way of adjusting one of four things: how hot the source runs, how much of the food's view it fills, how readily the surface accepts what arrives, and how long that surface is exposed before you move it, turn it, shield it, or take it away.

guides.safetyNote: Radiant cooking runs far hotter than the food ever gets: a charcoal bed sits near 800 to 1000 C, a broiler element near 900 C, and a wood oven dome near 400 C. Skin burns in under a second at those intensities and clothing can ignite, so keep bare forearms out of the direct beam, use dry cloths or leather gloves rather than wet ones (steam scalds instantly), and tie back hair and loose sleeves. Never add lighter fluid or any flammable liquid to lit coals. Fat dripping onto radiant elements causes flare-ups that can climb into a range hood, so keep a lid or a sheet pan within reach to smother flames and never use water on a grease fire. Cook all foods to safe internal temperatures measured with a probe, not by colour: 74 C for poultry and reheated leftovers, 71 C for ground meats, 63 C plus a three-minute rest for whole cuts of beef, pork and lamb, and 63 C for fish. Radiant heat browns the outside long before the centre is safe, so a black crust is not evidence of a cooked interior. Heavily charred meat carries polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and heterocyclic amines that are probable carcinogens; scrape off burnt deposits, avoid flare-ups, and do not eat carbonised material regularly. Run indoor broilers with ventilation, and never operate charcoal, gas or solid-fuel radiant cookers indoors, in a garage, or in a tent, because they emit carbon monoxide, which is odourless and kills.

guides.title: Dry Heat Versus Moist Heat Methods
guides.summary: A complete account of the two great families of cooking method — dry heat, which lets a surface climb past the boiling point of water and brown, and moist heat, which pins the food at or below about 100 °C and works by dissolving and softening. It covers the physics of heat transfer, the chemistry each family unlocks, every major technique in both, the combination methods that bridge them, and how to choose correctly for a given ingredient.

sections.heading: Why One Distinction Organizes the Whole Kitchen
sections.body: Almost every cooking method humans have invented sorts into one of two families, and the boundary between them is set by a single physical fact: whether liquid water is present in bulk at the food's surface. Where it is, the surface cannot get hotter than water's boiling point, about 100 °C at sea level. Where it is not, the surface is free to climb to 150 °C, 200 °C, 250 °C or beyond. That one number, and whether you are above or below it, decides which chemical reactions are available to you, what the food will taste like, what colour it will be, and which cuts of meat and which vegetables will be improved rather than ruined. Learning to see every technique through this lens turns a bewildering catalogue of named methods into two coherent systems with predictable behaviour. Dry-heat methods — roasting, baking, grilling, broiling, sautéing, pan-frying, deep-frying — drive the surface above the boiling point and therefore produce browning, crust, aroma compounds and concentrated flavour, at the cost of moisture loss and a steep internal temperature gradient. Moist-heat methods — boiling, simmering, poaching, steaming, sous vide, pressure cooking — hold the food at or below 100 °C, produce no browning at all, but transfer heat far more evenly, dissolve tough connective tissue into gelatin, and hydrate starches and pulses that dry heat would simply scorch. Neither family is superior. They do different jobs, and most of the classic dishes people consider difficult are really combination methods that use one family and then the other in sequence, in a deliberate order, for reasons that follow directly from the physics. The practical payoff of understanding this is diagnostic. When a roast chicken comes out pale and flabby, the reason is not a lack of skill but a surface that never got dry enough to exceed 100 °C, because evaporating moisture was consuming all the incoming energy. When a stew's beef is stringy and dry after three hours, the reason is not that it was cooked too long but that it was cooked too hot, boiling rather than barely trembling. When fried food is greasy, the oil was too cool, so steam pressure inside the food never stayed high enough to push oil back out. Each of these is a failure to respect what the presence or absence of water at the surface is doing. Once you can name the family you are working in and say what temperature the surface is actually reaching, you can predict the outcome before you commit the ingredient, and you can improvise methods you were never taught. That is the difference between following recipes and cooking.

sections.heading: Conduction, Convection and Radiation: How Heat Actually Arrives
sections.body: Heat reaches food by exactly three mechanisms, and every named technique is a particular blend of them. Conduction is direct contact: fast-moving molecules in a hot pan collide with slower molecules in the food's surface and hand over kinetic energy. It is the dominant mechanism in a skillet, on a griddle and inside the food itself, and it is fast where the contact is intimate and the material conducts well. Metals conduct enormously better than food does — copper carries heat roughly 400 watts per metre per kelvin, aluminium about 240, cast iron around 50, stainless steel only about 15, while a piece of meat manages roughly 0.4 to 0.5, close to water. That last figure is the reason thick cuts cook slowly no matter how fierce the fire: the food itself is the bottleneck, an insulator that must pass heat inward at its own stubborn pace. Convection is transport by a moving fluid, whether that fluid is air, steam, water or oil. Hot fluid carries energy to the surface, gives it up, becomes cooler and denser, sinks, and is replaced. The speed of this exchange depends heavily on the fluid. Still air is a poor carrier; a fan-forced oven moves air fast enough to cut cooking times by roughly a fifth and lets most recipes be run about 20 °C lower than in a conventional oven. Water is dramatically better than air, which is why a person can hold a hand in a 120 °C oven for a second or two but would be scalded instantly by 100 °C water. Water's volumetric heat capacity is more than three thousand times that of air, so it both holds far more energy and delivers it far more aggressively. This is the single most useful comparison in the kitchen: air at 200 °C is gentler on a surface than water at 100 °C, even though it is twice as hot on a thermometer. Radiation is energy carried by infrared electromagnetic waves, needing no medium at all. It is what you feel standing near glowing charcoal, what a broiler or salamander delivers, and what browns the top of a gratin. Radiant transfer rises with the fourth power of the source's absolute temperature, which is why charcoal at around 700 °C is not merely twice as fierce as an oven element at 300 °C but many times so, and why grilling can char an exterior in seconds while the interior stays raw. Real methods mix all three. An oven roast receives radiation from the walls, convection from circulating air, and conduction from the pan. Knowing which mechanism dominates tells you what to change: move the rack for radiation, open or close the door for convection, change the pan for conduction.

sections.heading: The Hundred-Degree Ceiling and Why Water Rules Everything
sections.body: Water behaves as a thermostat, and understanding that single behaviour explains most of what separates the two families of cooking. When liquid water is heated at ordinary atmospheric pressure, its temperature rises until it reaches roughly 100 °C, and then it stops rising. Further energy does not raise the temperature; it converts liquid into vapour. The energy required for that conversion, the latent heat of vaporisation, is enormous — about 2,260 kilojoules per kilogram, more than five times the energy needed to heat the same water from freezing to boiling in the first place. As long as free water remains at a food's surface and is evaporating, incoming heat is being spent on that phase change rather than on raising surface temperature. The surface is effectively pinned near 100 °C, and the reactions that need higher temperatures simply cannot start. This is why a wet steak in a hot pan hisses, steams and stays grey. It is why a chicken taken straight from a brine and put in the oven browns poorly while one air-dried uncovered in a refrigerator overnight browns beautifully. It is why patting things dry, salting them in advance to draw out and then reabsorb moisture, and not crowding the pan are not fussy chef affectations but direct manipulations of the energy budget. Crowding matters because each additional piece of food adds surface area shedding water vapour, and once the released vapour cannot escape fast enough the local atmosphere saturates, evaporation slows, and the pan's temperature crashes. You have accidentally built a steamer. The ceiling is not absolutely fixed. Boiling point falls with altitude, dropping roughly 1 °C per 285 metres of elevation, so water boils near 93 °C in Denver at about 1,600 metres and near 86 °C at 4,000 metres, which is why high-altitude cooks find beans and pasta take substantially longer. Pressure raises it: a domestic pressure cooker running at about one atmosphere of gauge pressure, or roughly 100 kilopascals above ambient, boils water at about 121 °C, which is enough to start browning reactions and is why pressure-cooked stocks and stews taste noticeably more roasted than simmered ones. Dissolved solutes raise it a little too, though far less than folklore suggests: salting pasta water to a palatable concentration lifts the boiling point by only a few tenths of a degree, so salt is added for seasoning, not for speed. Fats and sugars have no such ceiling at kitchen temperatures, which is precisely why oil and sugar syrups can reach 180 °C or 190 °C and become the vehicles for frying and caramel work. Every dry-heat technique is, at bottom, a scheme for getting a surface past water's ceiling.

sections.heading: Browning: The Maillard Reaction and Caramelization
sections.body: The prize that dry heat buys is browning, and browning is two distinct chemistries that are commonly confused. The Maillard reaction, described in 1912 by the French physician and chemist Louis-Camille Maillard, is a reaction between amino acids — the building blocks of protein — and reducing sugars such as glucose, fructose and lactose. It begins with a condensation that forms an unstable glycosylamine, rearranges through what is called the Amadori pathway, and then fragments and recombines through hundreds of branching routes into a vast family of new molecules: pyrazines that smell roasted and nutty, furans that smell caramel-like and sweet, thiophenes and thiazoles that smell meaty, and finally brown nitrogenous polymers called melanoidins that supply the colour. A single browned steak crust contains hundreds of aroma compounds that were simply not present in the raw meat. This is why browning is not cosmetic. It is the creation of flavour that did not exist before. Maillard chemistry proceeds slowly at low temperatures and accelerates sharply above roughly 140 °C to 150 °C, which is the practical threshold quoted in most kitchens. It is not a hard switch — the reaction runs at 100 °C given hours, which is why long-simmered condensed milk becomes dulce de leche and why pressure-cooked stock browns — but at ordinary cooking timescales, 140 °C is the line. The rate also depends strongly on water activity and pH. A surface soaked in water cannot exceed 100 °C and so barely browns; a surface that is bone dry browns fast. Alkaline conditions accelerate the reaction markedly, which is the reason pretzels are dipped in lye or a strong baking-soda solution before baking, why a pinch of bicarbonate helps onions caramelize in a fraction of the usual time, and why alkaline noodles brown so readily. Caramelization is a different process entirely: sugar decomposing under heat with no amino acid involved. Each sugar has its own onset — fructose begins near 110 °C, glucose near 150 °C, sucrose near 160 °C to 170 °C — and as the sugar breaks apart it produces diacetyl for butteriness, furans and maltol for sweetness and toastiness, and eventually bitter, dark polymers. Push it past roughly 190 °C and it turns acrid and black. Most real cooking runs both reactions at once, because most foods contain both protein and sugar. A roasting onion caramelizes its own fructose and glucose while also running Maillard chemistry with its amino acids. One important caveat belongs here honestly: high-temperature browning also generates compounds of health concern, including acrylamide in starchy foods above about 120 °C and heterocyclic amines and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in meat charred over flame. Official guidance in Europe and North America is to aim for golden rather than dark brown on starchy foods, and to avoid heavily blackened meat. The advice is moderation, not abstinence, and the evidence base is drawn largely from animal studies at high doses.

sections.heading: What Heat Does to Protein, Collagen and Fat
sections.body: Meat is roughly three-quarters water, held inside long muscle-fibre cells that are bundled and wrapped in sheets of connective tissue. Heat rearranges all three components, and it does so on a schedule precise enough to be worth memorising. Myosin, one of the two main contractile proteins, begins to denature — to unfold from its coiled native shape and tangle with its neighbours — at around 50 °C. This is what turns translucent raw flesh opaque and firm, and it is where a steak becomes rare. Actin, the other contractile protein, holds out until about 66 °C, and when it denatures the fibres contract hard and squeeze out a large fraction of their held water. That single transition is why a steak taken from 60 °C to 71 °C loses so dramatically more juice and reads as dry rather than merely well done. Myoglobin, the pigment that makes red meat red, loses its colour progressively and is essentially fully denatured near 71 °C to 74 °C. Connective tissue behaves oppositely, and the tension between the two behaviours is the entire drama of meat cookery. Collagen, the structural protein of tendon and the sheets around muscle bundles, is a triple helix that begins to shrink violently at roughly 60 °C to 65 °C, tightening like a drawstring and expelling juice. Held wet and hot for long enough, though, that shrunken collagen hydrolyses — breaks apart by reaction with water — into gelatin, which is soft, dissolves into the surrounding liquid, and gives braises their lip-coating richness. Conversion is slow at 70 °C and brisk at 85 °C to 95 °C. So a cut full of collagen must be taken far past the temperature at which its muscle fibres have already dried out, and it is the gelatin and the surrounding liquid that make the result taste succulent anyway. A cut with little collagen has nothing to gain from that treatment and everything to lose, which is the whole reason tender cuts are cooked hot and fast and tough cuts are cooked wet and slow. Fat plays a third role. It does not denature; it melts, over a range rather than at a point. Beef fat softens broadly between about 35 °C and 50 °C, pork a little lower, lamb higher, and this melting is what makes marbled meat feel juicy even when its water content has fallen. Rendering also liberates flavour: many of the compounds people identify as the characteristic taste of a given animal are fat-soluble and only become available once the fat has melted. In connective-tissue-rich cuts, rendering and collagen conversion happen over the same long window, which is why a properly braised shoulder tastes richer than the sum of its parts while a braised fillet tastes of nothing much at all.

sections.heading: Starch, Pectin and the Plant Side of the Question
sections.body: Plant foods respond to the two families along completely different lines from meat, and the governing structures are starch granules and the pectin that cements plant cells together. Starch in its raw state is packed into semi-crystalline granules that are largely indigestible and taste of chalk. Add water and heat and the granules undergo gelatinization: water forces its way into the crystalline regions, the granule swells to many times its original volume, and eventually it ruptures and releases long amylose chains that thicken the surrounding liquid. The onset temperature depends on the plant — wheat starch begins around 52 °C to 60 °C, potato around 58 °C to 66 °C, maize around 62 °C to 72 °C, rice around 68 °C to 78 °C — and the process is essentially complete somewhat above those ranges. Crucially, gelatinization requires water. This is why rice, pasta, beans and potatoes are cooked by moist heat: without free water there is nothing to swell the granules, and dry heat would simply toast and then burn the outside while the inside stayed raw. Dry heat does something quite different to starch. Above about 150 °C to 180 °C, and in the absence of enough water to gelatinize, starch fragments into shorter chains in a process called dextrinization, producing the nutty toasted flavour of a dark roux, of toasted flour, of the crust of a loaf. Baking a loaf of bread runs both processes simultaneously in different regions: the interior crumb stays close to 100 °C and gelatinizes, while the exterior dries out, climbs to 150 °C or more, and dextrinizes and browns. That single object is a compact demonstration of the whole dry-versus-moist distinction. Pectin is the other lever. It is a polysaccharide that acts as glue in the middle lamella between plant cells, and its breakdown is what turns a hard carrot tender. Pectin degrades by a reaction called beta-elimination that becomes significant above roughly 80 °C to 85 °C and runs faster in alkaline conditions and much slower in acid. This has direct practical consequences that surprise people. Beans cooked in a tomato or vinegar-heavy liquid stay stubbornly firm for hours, because acid stabilises the pectin; add the acid at the end instead. A pinch of bicarbonate in the cooking water softens beans and vegetables dramatically faster, at the cost of a slippery texture, some loss of thiamine and a duller green. Calcium has the opposite effect, cross-linking pectin and firming texture, which is why hard water slows bean cooking and why calcium chloride is added to canned tomatoes and pickles to keep them crisp. Cell walls also contain cellulose and hemicellulose, which ordinary cooking barely touches; the tenderness you achieve is almost entirely a pectin story.

sections.heading: Roasting and Baking: Dry Heat in Still or Moving Air
sections.body: Roasting and baking are the same physical process, and the two words are separated only by custom: meat and whole vegetables are roasted, doughs and batters and casseroles are baked. Both surround the food with hot air in an enclosed chamber, typically between 150 °C and 250 °C, so heat arrives by convection from the air, radiation from the oven walls and elements, and conduction from whatever the food sits on. Because air carries so little energy per unit volume, roasting is inherently gentle and slow at the surface, which is exactly what makes it forgiving. There is time for the interior to catch up before the exterior burns. The great variable is airflow. A conventional oven relies on natural convection, in which air rises as it warms, and the resulting circulation is sluggish; a real temperature gradient of 20 °C or more between top and bottom of the cavity is normal, and the hottest zone is usually the top rear. A fan-forced or convection oven adds a blower, which strips away the insulating boundary layer of saturated air clinging to the food's surface. The result is faster heat transfer and, more importantly, faster moisture removal, so surfaces dry and brown sooner. The standard conversion is to drop the set temperature by about 20 °C and expect roughly 20 to 25 percent shorter times, but the more useful mental model is that a fan makes the oven more aggressive at drying, which is excellent for roast potatoes and crisp-skinned poultry and unhelpful for delicate custards and some cakes, where a fan can set a skin before the centre has risen. Technique follows from the physics. Elevating a roast on a rack lets air reach the underside so the whole surface browns rather than stewing in its own exuded juice. Leaving space between items keeps the local air from saturating. Starting a large roast at a high temperature to establish colour and then dropping to 150 °C or lower, or the reverse — a long low cook followed by a short blast — both work, and the low-then-high order generally gives a more evenly cooked interior because the food spends less total time in the steep gradient. Carryover cooking is a real and often mishandled effect: a large roast pulled from the oven continues to rise, typically 3 °C to 8 °C depending on mass and oven temperature, as heat migrates inward from the hot exterior. Pull a beef rib roast at about 52 °C to serve it at medium rare. Resting matters for the same reason and for a second one: during rest the steep internal pressure gradient relaxes and denatured proteins reabsorb some expelled liquid, so a rested joint loses far less juice on carving. Ten minutes suits a steak, twenty to forty a large roast, loosely tented so the crust does not soften.

sections.heading: Grilling, Broiling and the Radiant Extreme
sections.body: Grilling and broiling occupy the violent end of the dry-heat family, where radiation dominates and surface temperatures are the highest a cook normally encounters. In grilling the heat source sits below the food; in broiling, which British kitchens call grilling, confusingly, the source sits above. Physically they are the same: an intensely hot emitter — glowing charcoal at 600 °C to 900 °C, a gas burner's ceramic radiants, or an electric element — throwing infrared energy directly onto the food. Radiant power scales with the fourth power of the emitter's absolute temperature under the Stefan–Boltzmann law, so doubling the source temperature in kelvin multiplies the delivered energy roughly sixteenfold. This is why the difference between a bed of charcoal at full roar and one that has faded is not incremental but categorical. That intensity is a tool with a narrow window. Surface temperatures on a grilled steak can exceed 300 °C, which browns in tens of seconds and chars in a minute or two, while the interior of a three-centimetre steak needs several minutes to reach 55 °C. For thin items — a lamb chop, a prawn, a flatbread, asparagus — the two timescales match and grilling is ideal. For thick items they do not, and the classic solution is a two-zone fire: a hot zone directly over the coals and a cool zone beside them with no fuel underneath. The food cooks through by convection and mild radiation on the cool side with the lid down, essentially being roasted, and is finished over the hot zone for colour. The reverse sear applies the same logic in an oven and then a pan. Grilling adds flavour that no other method produces, and it is worth being precise about where it comes from. It is not the fuel's smoke in any simple sense. Most of it is dripping fat and juice falling onto the hot surface below, vaporising and pyrolysing, and rising back as aromatic smoke that condenses on the food. This is also the origin of flare-ups, which are fat fires, and of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, the compounds that make heavy charring a genuine if modest health concern. Practical mitigations are trimming excess fat, avoiding sustained flame contact, moving food off flare-ups rather than spraying water, and not eating the blackest parts routinely. Distance is the cook's main control. Doubling the gap between food and emitter cuts the radiant flux roughly to a quarter, following the inverse-square relationship, so raising or lowering a grill grate or moving an oven rack one position under a broiler changes the browning rate far more than most people expect. Broiling in particular rewards attention: an item 8 centimetres from an element can go from pale to burnt in under sixty seconds, and there is no useful way to recover from that.

sections.heading: Sautéing, Pan-Frying and Searing on Metal
sections.body: Sautéing, pan-frying and searing are dry-heat methods in which conduction through a hot metal surface does most of the work and a thin film of fat acts as a thermal gasket. The fat is not there primarily to add flavour or to prevent sticking, though it does both. Its structural job is to fill the microscopic valleys between an irregular piece of food and an irregular pan so that contact is continuous rather than a scattering of touching high points. Without it, only a few percent of the nominal contact area is actually transferring heat. With it, a tablespoon of oil turns a rough interface into an effectively complete one, which is why a properly oiled pan browns evenly and a dry one produces leopard spots. The distinction between the named techniques is one of degree. Sautéing, from the French sauter, to jump, uses a small quantity of fat, high heat and small or thin pieces kept in motion; it suits mushrooms, sliced onions, prawns, cutlets. Pan-frying uses more fat, often to a depth of several millimetres, and moderate heat with less agitation, suiting thicker items and breaded coatings. Searing is simply the high-temperature browning stage, whether it opens a cook or closes it. All three depend on a surface temperature comfortably above 140 °C, and all three are defeated by the same two errors: wet food and a crowded pan. Both flood the pan with water that must be evaporated before anything can brown, and both drop the pan's temperature by drawing off the latent heat of vaporisation faster than the burner can replace it. Pan choice therefore matters in a specific, physical way. What you want is high thermal mass and good conductivity, so the pan resists the temperature crash when cold food lands. Cast iron and carbon steel are heavy and hold heat well but conduct unevenly, giving hot spots directly over a burner. Clad stainless with an aluminium or copper core spreads heat evenly but usually has less mass. Thin stainless alone is the worst of both. Preheating properly matters more than the metal: a pan should be brought up over two to four minutes and tested, either with the water-droplet test in which a drop skitters intact across the surface rather than sizzling and evaporating in place, indicating roughly 180 °C and the Leidenfrost effect, or simply with a shimmer in the oil. One persistent myth deserves burying. Searing does not seal in juices; that idea traces to Justus von Liebig in the 1840s and was disproved experimentally by the mid-twentieth century. Seared meat loses slightly more moisture than unseared meat, not less. Searing is done for flavour and colour, which is reason enough, and the fond — the browned residue stuck to the pan — is the basis of every pan sauce, released by deglazing with wine, stock or water.

sections.heading: Deep-Frying: A Dry Method Conducted in Liquid
sections.body: Deep-frying looks like a moist method and is emphatically a dry one, and resolving that apparent paradox explains why it works. The food is immersed in a liquid, but that liquid is fat, which has no boiling ceiling at kitchen temperatures. Frying oils are typically run between 160 °C and 190 °C, far above water's 100 °C, so the surface of the food dries, browns and crisps exactly as it would in an oven — only much faster, because oil is a vastly better convective medium than air. A fryer at 180 °C delivers heat to a surface perhaps twenty times faster than an oven at the same temperature. That speed is the entire point: the exterior can be driven to full crust before the interior has time to overcook. What happens inside a piece of frying food is a moving boundary. The surface loses its water first and rises to near the oil's temperature; a millimetre or two beneath, water is still boiling off at 100 °C; deeper still, the food is merely cooking. The vigorous bubbling you see is that steam escaping, and it is doing important work: the outward pressure of escaping vapour is what keeps oil from soaking in. This is the key to non-greasy fried food. While steam is streaming out, oil cannot stream in. Most oil absorption actually happens during cooling, as the food's interior contracts and draws oil into the pores of the crust, which is why draining on a rack rather than on paper in a pile, and salting immediately, matter. Temperature discipline is therefore everything. Oil that is too cool, below about 150 °C, produces feeble steam pressure, so oil penetrates and the result is heavy and greasy. Oil that is too hot, above about 200 °C for most purposes, burns the crust before the centre is done and degrades the oil itself. Adding food crashes the temperature, so batches should be small — a rough rule is no more than one part food to six parts oil by volume — and the oil should be allowed to recover between batches. A clip-on thermometer removes all guesswork and is the single best investment in frying. Smoke point sets the ceiling for oil choice: refined peanut, sunflower, canola, rice-bran and vegetable oils sit around 200 °C to 230 °C and are suitable; extra-virgin olive oil, butter and unrefined oils smoke far lower and are not. Oil degrades with use through hydrolysis, oxidation and polymerisation, darkening, thickening, foaming and smoking at ever-lower temperatures; discard it when it foams persistently, smells fishy or acrid, or has gone syrupy, which for home use is usually after three to six sessions. Coatings exist to manage the boundary. A batter or breadcrumb layer is a sacrificial shell that dries and browns while insulating the food beneath, which is why fish stays moist inside a crisp jacket. Starches high in amylose, and additions of rice flour, cornflour or vodka, produce crisper, less elastic crusts because they form fewer gluten networks and hold less water.

sections.heading: Boiling, Simmering and Poaching: The Moist Spectrum
sections.body: The moist-heat family begins with three techniques that differ only in water temperature, and the distinctions among them are far more consequential than their casual usage suggests. Boiling is a full rolling turbulence at 100 °C at sea level, with vigorous convection and continuous mechanical agitation from rising bubbles. Simmering runs at roughly 85 °C to 96 °C, with occasional bubbles breaking the surface and gentle movement. Poaching runs lower still, from about 70 °C to 85 °C, with no visible bubbling at all and only the faintest shiver on the surface — the French call the lowest version frémissement, a trembling. Because there is no browning available anywhere on this spectrum, the only variables that matter are temperature and turbulence, and both act primarily on texture. Turbulence is destructive. A rolling boil batters delicate items to pieces, which is why poached eggs, fish fillets, dumplings, quenelles and chicken breasts are ruined by it and saved by a bare shiver. Temperature is equally decisive for protein foods, because the same denaturation thresholds apply here as anywhere: a chicken breast poached at 75 °C emerges tender and moist, while the same breast boiled at 100 °C contracts hard, expels its water and turns to string. This is the single most useful correction most home cooks can make. Almost everything people describe as boiled meat should have been simmered or poached. Boiling proper is reserved for things that benefit from turbulence and speed and cannot be damaged by it: pasta, which needs vigorous movement to stop it clumping and enough thermal mass to recover temperature; green vegetables, which are best cooked briefly in a large volume of heavily salted water so the water does not cool and the vegetables do not sit long enough to lose colour; and potatoes and other dense starches, which need the full 100 °C to gelatinize throughout in reasonable time. Starting potatoes in cold water and bringing them up together avoids a mushy outside and raw centre, because the outside would otherwise be twenty minutes ahead. An important trade-off runs through all of it: water-soluble nutrients and flavour leach out. Boiling vegetables can cost 30 to 50 percent of their vitamin C and much of their B vitamins into the water, which is why steaming generally preserves more and why the cooking liquid is worth keeping when it suits the dish. That same leaching is a feature when you want it. Stock-making is deliberate, patient extraction: bones and aromatics held at a bare simmer, never boiled, for hours, so that collagen converts to gelatin and flavour migrates into the water while fat and scum stay separated at the top rather than being emulsified into cloudiness by turbulence. A boiled stock is a cloudy, greasy stock, every time.

sections.heading: Steaming, Pressure Cooking and Sous Vide
sections.body: Steaming suspends food above boiling water so that condensing vapour, not liquid, delivers the heat. It is a moist method with a distinctive advantage: because the food never sits in water, soluble vitamins, minerals and flavour compounds stay where they are rather than leaching out. Steamed broccoli retains substantially more vitamin C than boiled broccoli, and the difference is easy to taste as well as measure. The heat transfer is also surprisingly brisk, because condensation releases the full latent heat of vaporisation — about 2,260 kilojoules per kilogram — right at the food's surface. That is exactly why a steam burn is so much worse than a hot-water burn, and why lids should be lifted with the far edge tilted away from you. The steamer's temperature is fixed at 100 °C in an open vessel, so the technique is inherently gentle and self-limiting; the main risk is overcooking through time rather than through excess heat. It suits delicate proteins, dumplings, custards, vegetables and any dish where a dry surface would be a defect: dim sum, fish, puddings. It cannot brown, so it is often paired with a finishing sear, and it loses efficiency the moment steam can escape freely, which is why a heavy well-fitted lid matters more than the type of basket. Pressure cooking breaks the 100 °C ceiling by raising the pressure. A sealed vessel operating at about 100 kilopascals of gauge pressure, one extra atmosphere, boils water at roughly 121 °C; lower settings around 50 kilopascals give about 112 °C. That extra 15 to 20 degrees roughly halves or quarters cooking times, because chemical reaction rates broadly double for every 10 °C rise. Collagen converts in 45 minutes instead of three hours, dried beans cook in half an hour, stock reaches in one hour a depth that would take five. Critically, 121 °C is above the Maillard threshold, so pressure-cooked stocks and stews genuinely brown a little and taste roasted rather than merely boiled. The trade-offs are honest ones: fresh volatile aromas are driven off and lost, delicate items overcook invisibly because you cannot look, and food expands, so a pressure cooker must never be filled beyond two-thirds, or half for foaming foods such as beans, pulses, rice and pasta. Sous vide sits at the opposite extreme: food sealed in a pouch and held in a precisely controlled water bath, typically 50 °C to 90 °C, for hours. It is a moist method by every physical criterion, but because the bath is set to the target doneness the food can never exceed it. A steak held at 54.5 °C for two hours is edge-to-edge medium rare with no gradient at all. Tough cuts held at 60 °C to 65 °C for 24 to 72 hours convert collagen slowly enough that the muscle fibres never dry out. It cannot brown, so a hard fast sear afterwards is obligatory. Food-safety at these low temperatures depends on time as well as temperature; published pasteurisation tables, not intuition, are the correct authority.

sections.heading: Combination Methods: Braising, Stewing and Pot-Roasting
sections.body: The most satisfying dishes in most cuisines are neither dry nor moist but both, applied in a deliberate order. Braising means browning a large piece of meat by dry heat and then cooking it partly submerged in liquid at a bare simmer, covered, for hours. Stewing is the same logic applied to small pieces fully submerged. Pot-roasting sits between them, using very little liquid. In every case the dry stage is done first and cannot be done later, because once the surface is wet it can never exceed 100 °C again. The browning stage buys the Maillard compounds; the wet stage buys collagen conversion. Skip the first and the dish tastes flat and grey; skip the second and the meat stays tough. The order is not tradition, it is physics. The target temperature for the wet stage is the most commonly botched detail. It should sit around 85 °C to 95 °C, never a boil, which usually means an oven at 140 °C to 160 °C rather than a hob, since an oven surrounds the pot and holds a steady, gentle state without scorching the base. At those temperatures collagen hydrolyses steadily to gelatin over two to four hours while the muscle fibres, already fully contracted, sit in a bath of liquid rich enough to eat as sauce. Cuts to choose are the hard-working ones: beef chuck, shin and oxtail, lamb shoulder and shanks, pork shoulder, chicken thighs and legs. Lean tender cuts have nothing to give and simply dry out.
steps: Dry the meat thoroughly with paper and season it well; any surface moisture will steam rather than brown and cost you the entire first stage.

Heat a heavy pot with a tight lid over medium-high heat, add a thin film of a high-smoke-point oil, and brown the meat hard on every face without crowding, working in batches so the pot never cools below browning temperature.
Remove the meat, lower the heat, and cook the aromatic vegetables in the same fat until they colour, scraping to keep the fond from burning.
Deglaze with wine, stock, beer or water, scraping every browned trace off the base — that fond is a large fraction of the finished flavour.
Return the meat, add liquid to come between one third and two thirds of the way up for a braise or to cover for a stew, and bring to a bare simmer on the hob.
Cover and transfer to an oven at 150 °C, checking after an hour that the liquid is trembling and not bubbling; drop the oven 10 to 20 °C if it is.
Cook two to four hours until a fork meets no resistance, then rest the meat in its liquid, skim the fat, and reduce the sauce hard on the hob if it needs concentrating.

sections.heading: Matching the Method to the Ingredient, and the Kit It Needs
sections.body: Choosing correctly comes down to two questions asked in order. First, does this ingredient hold enough connective tissue that it needs long wet cooking to become tender? Second, can it brown before its interior is spoiled? The answers point at a family almost automatically. A beef fillet has almost no collagen and is tender raw, so wet heat can only harm it; it wants fast dry heat and 52 °C to 57 °C inside. A beef shin is nothing but collagen and wants three hours at 90 °C in liquid. A chicken breast is lean and wants gentle dry heat or poaching to 74 °C, while a thigh carries enough collagen and fat to improve anywhere from 75 °C to 90 °C. Fish inverts several rules, because its connective tissue is a far more fragile collagen that converts to gelatin at only about 50 °C. That is why fish flakes apart at the slightest overcooking, why most fish is best pulled between 50 °C and 60 °C, and why it wants fast dry heat or gentle poaching. Eggs are a temperature map of their own: white sets between about 62 °C and 65 °C, yolk thickens near 65 °C, and a whole egg scrambled above 75 °C weeps water, which is why low heat gives creamy curds while high heat gives rubber. Vegetables split by density and starch. Green vegetables lose colour fast and want a short violent boil or a hot sear, both of which finish before degradation sets in. Dense roots and brassicas reward dry heat, because roasting drives off water to concentrate sugars and adds browning on top; the same carrot boiled is merely soft, roasted it is deeply flavoured. Starchy staples — rice, pasta, dried beans, lentils, polenta — are moist-heat foods without exception, because gelatinization and the hydration of dried pulses both require free water that no oven can supply. Equipment follows from the same physics. Fat choice is governed by smoke point: refined oils above 200 °C belong to hot dry work, while butter's milk solids brown near 150 °C and burn soon after, which is why clarified butter and ghee tolerate roughly 250 °C. Above all, treat the lid as a switch between the two families, since it traps the food's own steam and turns any pan into a moist-heat chamber.
ingredients: A refined neutral oil with a smoke point above 200 °C — peanut, canola, rice-bran or sunflower — for searing and frying; any supermarket, cheapest in large bottles.
Clarified butter or ghee for browning at high heat with dairy flavour; sold in jars in South Asian shops, or made at home by melting butter and skimming.
A heavy skillet with real thermal mass: cast iron or carbon steel, 26 to 30 cm; carbon steel is lighter and heats faster, cast iron holds heat better.
A heavy lidded casserole or Dutch oven, 4 to 6 litres, for braises, stews and stocks.
A fast-read digital probe thermometer, plus a clip-on fryer thermometer if you deep-fry.
A fire blanket or a metal lid large enough to smother a pan, kept within reach of the hob.

sections.heading: Doneness, Time-at-Temperature and Food Safety
sections.body: Safety in cooking is a function of temperature and time together, not temperature alone, and the familiar single numbers on packaging are simply the points at which the required reduction in pathogens happens almost instantly. Poultry is quoted at 74 °C, ground meats at 71 °C, and whole cuts of beef, pork, veal and lamb at 63 °C with a three-minute rest, all measured with a probe in the thickest part away from bone. Those figures come from pasteurisation tables that express equivalent lethality: chicken held at 60 °C for about 35 minutes achieves the same reduction in salmonella as chicken flashed to 74 °C, which is exactly why low-temperature and sous vide cooking is safe when it is done with a controlled bath and a published table, and unsafe when it is improvised. Whole intact cuts of red meat are a special case worth understanding. Contamination on them is essentially confined to the surface, because muscle interiors are sterile in a healthy animal, so a seared exterior sterilises the only part that was at risk and a rare interior is safe. Grinding distributes surface bacteria throughout, which is the entire reason minced meat requires a higher internal temperature than the steak it was cut from. Mechanically tenderised or needle-injected cuts must be treated like ground meat for the same reason. The temperature danger zone, from 5 °C to 60 °C, is where most bacteria multiply fastest, and the standard rule is that food should spend no more than two hours cumulatively within it, dropping to one hour above 32 °C ambient. That clock runs across the whole life of the food, so slow cooling after cooking counts. Cool large volumes fast by dividing them into shallow containers, and refrigerate within two hours rather than leaving a pot on the stove overnight. Reheating should take food back through the zone quickly and to at least 74 °C. Doneness for eating quality is a separate judgement with its own numbers. Beef and lamb: 52 °C rare, 57 °C medium rare, 63 °C medium, above 68 °C well done and progressively dry. Pork is safe at 63 °C and is far better there than at the 71 °C once demanded, a change reflecting the effective elimination of trichinella from commercial herds. Chicken breast dries above 74 °C; thighs are better at 80 °C to 85 °C where their collagen softens. Fish is generally best at 50 °C to 60 °C. Remember carryover: pull a large roast 3 °C to 8 °C below target, a thin steak 2 °C to 3 °C below, and let the residual gradient finish the job during the rest.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Hard Limits and How to Recover
sections.body: Most kitchen disasters are one of a short list of failures, and each has a diagnosis that follows directly from the two-family model. Food that will not brown is almost always wet, crowded or too cool. The remedy is to dry the surface thoroughly, cook in smaller batches, and preheat properly; adding more heat to a crowded wet pan only produces more steam. Food that browns but stays raw inside has the opposite problem: the surface heat flux is far too high for the thickness. Move it further from the source, lower the temperature, or split the cook into a gentle stage and a colouring stage. Meat that is tough after long cooking is almost never undercooked; it has usually been cooked too hot, boiled rather than simmered, so the fibres have been wrung out faster than the collagen could convert. The recovery is genuine: drop the temperature to a bare tremble, add liquid, and continue, often for another hour or more, and much of the texture will come back as gelatin accumulates. Meat that is tough after fast cooking is a different failure entirely, an inappropriate cut, and it cannot be rescued by more of the same heat — the only route is to slice it thinly across the grain, or dice it and start a wet cook. Greasy fried food means the oil was too cool or the batches were too big. Soggy roast vegetables mean a crowded tray and trapped steam; spread them out and raise the heat. Curdled or grainy egg sauces mean the proteins passed roughly 80 °C and coagulated; sometimes whisking in a spoonful of cold liquid off the heat will bring them back, often not. Split braising sauces usually just need skimming and reducing. Burnt fond at the base of a pot is unrecoverable and will taint everything; transfer the contents to a clean pot without scraping and accept the loss. The honest limits are worth stating plainly. Nothing browns below 100 °C at ordinary kitchen timescales, so no covered wet pot will ever produce a crust. Nothing gelatinizes starch or hydrates a dried bean without free water, so no oven will cook rice properly without added liquid. No amount of resting repairs meat taken to 80 °C internally. Carryover cannot be reversed. And the most dangerous limit is a fat fire: if oil ignites, cut the heat and smother it with a lid or blanket, never water, never by carrying the pan, and evacuate and call emergency services if it is not out within seconds. When a dish is failing, the productive question is always the same one: what temperature is the surface actually at, and is there water on it?

guides.safetyNote: Hot fat is the most dangerous thing in a domestic kitchen: cooking oils smoke between roughly 160 °C and 230 °C depending on type and reach their autoignition point around 315–370 °C, and a fat fire must NEVER be doused with water — the water flashes to steam and throws burning oil across the room. Smother it with a lid or a fire blanket and turn off the heat. Steam causes far worse burns than dry air at the same temperature because it releases about 2,260 kilojoules per kilogram as it condenses on skin, so open lids and pressure cookers away from your face and hands. Never add wet food to deep fat. Separately, browning and moisture control are not substitutes for temperature control: poultry must reach 74 °C, ground meats 71 °C, and whole cuts of beef, pork and lamb 63 °C followed by a three-minute rest, measured with a probe thermometer in the thickest part, and food should not sit between 5 °C and 60 °C for more than two hours in total.

guides.title: The Fifteen Classical Cooking Methods Compared
guides.summary: A mechanism-first comparison of the fifteen classical cooking methods, from roasting and grilling through frying, poaching, and steaming to braising and stewing, explaining how each moves heat, what chemistry it triggers, which foods it suits, and how to diagnose its failures.

sections.heading: Why the Cooking Method Matters More Than the Recipe
sections.body: Nearly everything humans cook is transformed by one of a small family of techniques that professional kitchens codified more than a century ago.
